adj:gram.tx: From Middle High German gram, from Old High German gram, from Proto-Germanic *gramaz.

verb:geben.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gëben, from Old High German gëban, from Proto-West Germanic *geban, from Proto-Germanic *gebaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-.

adj:gut.tx: Inherited from Middle High German guot, from Old High German guot, from Proto-West Germanic *gōd, from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, be associated, suit”). Cognates Cognate to Luxembourgish gutt, Silesian East Central German gutt, Dutch goed, West Frisian goed, Saterland Frisian goud, English good, Danish god, Norwegian god and Swedish god.

adv:gut.tx: Inherited from Middle High German guot, from Old High German guot, from Proto-West Germanic *gōd, from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, be associated, suit”). Cognates Cognate to Luxembourgish gutt, Silesian East Central German gutt, Dutch goed, West Frisian goed, Saterland Frisian goud, English good, Danish god, Norwegian god and Swedish god.

intj:gut.tx: Inherited from Middle High German guot, from Old High German guot, from Proto-West Germanic *gōd, from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, be associated, suit”). Cognates Cognate to Luxembourgish gutt, Silesian East Central German gutt, Dutch goed, West Frisian goed, Saterland Frisian goud, English good, Danish god, Norwegian god and Swedish god.

verb:glauben.tx: From Middle High German gelouben, gelöuben, from Old High German gilouben, from Proto-West Germanic *galaubijan, from Proto-Germanic *galaubijaną. The form with -au- is Upper German; it was reinforced by the related noun Glaube against the Central German variant with umlaut. Compare however gläubig and abergläubisch. Cognate with Bavarian glaubn, glabn, Dutch geloven, Low German glöven, Gothic …

adj:gewöhnlich.tx: From Middle High German gewon(e)lich, from Old High German giwonalīh (11th c. as adverb giwonalīhho), from Proto-West Germanic *gawunalīk. Cognate with Dutch gewoonlijk, Old English ġewuneliċ. Equivalent to gewohn + -lich, the former being an obsolete variant of gewohnt. The umlaut in Modern German developed under influence of related gewöhnen (Middle High German gewenen).

adv:gewöhnlich.tx: From Middle High German gewon(e)lich, from Old High German giwonalīh (11th c. as adverb giwonalīhho), from Proto-West Germanic *gawunalīk. Cognate with Dutch gewoonlijk, Old English ġewuneliċ. Equivalent to gewohn + -lich, the former being an obsolete variant of gewohnt. The umlaut in Modern German developed under influence of related gewöhnen (Middle High German gewenen).

noun:Gaul.tx: From Middle High German gūl, from Old High German *gūl, from Proto-West Germanic *gūl- (stem form uncertain). Cognate with Dutch guil, Middle Low German gûl(e). Further origin obscure, but possibly related with gießen (“to pour”), referring to a “seed pourer”, that is a stud.

noun:Geist.tx: From Middle High German geist, from Old High German geist, from Proto-West Germanic *gaist, from Proto-Germanic *gaistaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰóysdos (“anger, agitation”). Cognate with Dutch geest, West Frisian geast, English ghost, Swedish gast, Persian زشت (zešt, “ugly, hateful, disgusting”).

noun:Gewicht.tx: From Middle High German wiht, gewiht, from Old High German giwihti, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *gawihtī. Compare Dutch gewicht, Danish vægt, English weight, Swedish vikt.

noun:Gabel.tx: From Middle High German gabel(e), from Old High German gabala, from Proto-West Germanic *gabulu (“fork”).

noun:Garten.tx: From Middle High German garte, from Old High German garto, from Proto-West Germanic *gardō. Cognate with Dutch gaarde, English yard, and through a Romance borrowing from Frankish: English garden, French jardin, Spanish jardín, Italian giardino. Also, cognate with Proto-Slavic *gȏrdъ, shifted to Russian город (gorod), Polish gród or Czech hrad.

adj:ganz.tx: From Middle High German ganz, from Old High German ganz (“whole, sound, healthy, complete, fullstanding”), from Proto-West Germanic *gant (“whole, sound”).

adv:ganz.tx: From Middle High German ganz, from Old High German ganz (“whole, sound, healthy, complete, fullstanding”), from Proto-West Germanic *gant (“whole, sound”).

adj:grün.tx: From Middle High German grüene, from Old High German gruoni, gruoen, from Proto-West Germanic *grōnī, from Proto-Germanic *grōniz. Compare Low German grön, Dutch groen, English green, Danish grøn.

adj:gar.tx: From Middle High German gare (inflected garw-), from Old High German garo, from Proto-West Germanic *garu, from Proto-Germanic *garwaz. Cognate with Dutch gaar, archaic English yare (“keen, lively, eager”). Related to gerben.

adv:gar.tx: From Middle High German gare (inflected garw-), from Old High German garo, from Proto-West Germanic *garu, from Proto-Germanic *garwaz. Cognate with Dutch gaar, archaic English yare (“keen, lively, eager”). Related to gerben.

noun:Gesundheit.tx: From Middle High German gesuntheit. By surface analysis, gesund (“healthy”) + -heit (“-ness, -hood”). Compare Dutch gezondheid.

intj:Gesundheit.tx: From Middle High German gesuntheit. By surface analysis, gesund (“healthy”) + -heit (“-ness, -hood”). Compare Dutch gezondheid.

adj:groß.tx: From Middle High German grōȥ, from Old High German grōȥ, akin to Old Saxon grōt, compare Dutch groot. More at English great.

verb:gehen.tx: From Middle High German gān, gēn, from Old High German gān, gēn, from Proto-West Germanic *gān, from Proto-Germanic *gāną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave”). Cognate with Dutch gaan, Low German gaan, gahn, English go, Swedish and Danish gå, Yiddish גיין (geyn). The form gēn instead of gān is of Bavarian origin, but many dialects of Central and Low German have -e- (from earlier -ei-) …

noun:Gefühl.tx: Apparently not attested before the 17th century. Derived from ge- + fühlen; compare Gehör, Gesicht (both older). Perhaps a calque of Dutch gevoel. This is slightly earlier (16th c., doubtfully in 1450) and moreover Middle Dutch already made ample use of the nominalized infinitive gevoelen. Earlier High German words were Fühle f (now obsolete) and Fühlung (now in a different sense).

adj:golden.tx: Common since the 18th century. Alteration (after Gold (“gold”)) of older gulden, gülden, from Middle High German guldīn, güldīn, from Old High German guldīn, from Proto-Germanic *gulþīnaz. Equivalent to Gold + -en. Cognate with Dutch gulden, gouden, English golden.

verb:gehören.tx: From Middle High German gehœren (“listen to, obey”), from Old High German gihōrian (“to hearken to”), from Proto-West Germanic *gahauʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *gahauzijaną (compare Old English ġehīeran, Old Saxon gihōrian, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (gahausjan)). By surface analysis, ge- + hören. Compare with English hear.

noun:Geburtstag.tx: From Middle High German geburttac, from Old High German giburtitag, from Proto-West Germanic *gaburdidag; equivalent to Geburt (“birth”) + -s- + Tag (“day”).

adv:gestern.tx: From Middle High German gestern, from Old High German gesteron, gesteren, from Proto-West Germanic *gesteran. Cognate with English yester, Dutch gisteren.

noun:Gruß.tx: From Middle High German gruoȥ; compare Dutch groet. See German grüßen.

noun:Gattung.tx: From Middle High German gatunge, from gaten (“to come together, to fit”), from Old High German (bi)gaton, from Proto-West Germanic *gadōn. Cognate with Dutch gading (“satisfaction”).

noun:Gülle.tx: From Middle High German gülle (“puddle”), see the Swiss German entry above.

adj:genial.tx: Clipping of earlier genialisch. Compare French génial, Spanish genial.

adj:gleich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gelīch, from Old High German gilīh, from Proto-West Germanic *galīk, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.

adv:gleich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gelīch, from Old High German gilīh, from Proto-West Germanic *galīk, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.

noun:Gold.tx: From Middle High German golt, from Old High German gold, from Proto-West Germanic *golþ, from Proto-Germanic *gulþą.

noun:Gabe.tx: From geben (“give”), also inherited from Middle High German gābe, from Old High German *gāba, from Proto-West Germanic *gābā, from Proto-Germanic *gēbǭ (“gift, giving”), from *gebaną whence English give.

noun:Gambit.tx: Borrowed from Spanish gambito, from Italian gambetto.

noun:Gang.tx: From Middle High German ganc, from Old High German gang, from Proto-West Germanic *gang. Cognate with English gang.

noun:Gans.tx: From Middle High German gans, from Old High German gans, from Proto-West Germanic *gans, from Proto-Germanic *gans, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns. Compare Low German Gans, Goos, Dutch gans, English goose, Danish gås.

noun:Garage.tx: Borrowed from French garage in the early 1900s. Compare Hunsrik Garaasch.

noun:Gas.tx: From Dutch gas. Doublet of Chaos.

noun:Gast.tx: From Middle High German gast, from Old High German gast, from Proto-West Germanic *gasti, from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis. Germanic cognates include Dutch gast, English guest, Old Norse gestr (whence Swedish gäst, Danish gæst, Norwegian Nynorsk gjest, Norwegian Bokmål gjest, Icelandic gestur), and Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍃𐍄𐍃 (gasts). Indo-European cognates include Latin hostis …

noun:Gazelle.tx: Borrowed from Italian gazzella, from Arabic غَزَال (ḡazāl).

noun:Gecko.tx: Borrowed from Dutch gekko, further possibly from Malay [Term?] or Acehnese [Term?]. Compare English gecko for more.

noun:Gel.tx: 20th century, borrowed (with a spelling pronunciation) from English gel, itself coined by 19th-century chemist Thomas Graham. Analysable as a clipping of Gelatine, but note that the latter is mostly realized with /ʒ/, which Gel never is.

noun:Geld.tx: From Middle High German gëlt, from Old High German gëlt, këlt, from Proto-West Germanic *geld, from Proto-Germanic *geldą (“reward, gift, money”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”). The modern consonantism -d instead of expected -t is Central and Low German (compare Middle Low German gelt, -des, from Old Saxon geld); but also Upper German in some dialects through revoicing after -l-. …

noun:General.tx: Partly via Middle High German general, partly via French général, from Latin generālis.

noun:Genie.tx: Borrowed from French génie, from Latin genius.

noun:Genre.tx: Borrowed from French genre. Doublet of Genus and Gender.

noun:Germanium.tx: Coined by German chemist Clemens Winkler in 1886, from Latin Germania + -ium, in honour of his nation.

noun:Gift.tx: From Middle High German gift f (“gift, present”), Old High German gift f (“gift”), from Proto-West Germanic *gifti, from Proto-Germanic *giftiz, which is a derivation of *gebaną (“to give”). Cognate with English gift. The word has been used as a euphemism for "poison" since Old High German, a semantic loan from Late Latin dosis (“dose”), from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “gift; dose of medicine”). …

noun:Gin.tx: Borrowed from English gin, from Dutch genever, from Latin iūniperus. Doublet of Genever.

noun:Giraffe.tx: From Middle High German geraff, seraffe, schraffe, partly via Italian giraffa, partly directly (in travel reports) from Arabic زَرافَة (zarāfa).

noun:Glas.tx: From Old High German glas, gles, from Proto-West Germanic *glas, from Proto-Germanic *glasą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- (“to shine, glimmer, glow”). Compare Low German Glas, Dutch glas, English glass, Icelandic gler.

noun:Glottis.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin glottis, from Ancient Greek γλωττίς (glōttís).

noun:Glut.tx: From Middle High German gluot, from Old High German gluot, from Proto-Germanic *glōdiz. Cognates include English gleed, Dutch gloed, Icelandic glóð, Swedish glöd.

noun:Gluten.tx: Ultimately from Latin glūten. The usual pronunciation apparently by analogy with chemical terms in -en (“-ene”).

noun:Gnu.tx: First used by Georg Forster in 1778, transcribing English gnoo, which he himself had introduced, a year earlier, in his English work A voyage round the world. Further from Khoekhoe !nu:, possibly via South African Dutch. While Dutch gnoe is only attested later on (common Afrikaans being wildebees), it may nevertheless have existed because it would have been difficult for Forster to borrow the …

noun:Golf.tx: Borrowed from Italian golfo, from Late Latin colfus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos). See gulf.

noun:Grab.tx: From Middle High German grap, from Old High German grap, from Proto-West Germanic *grab, from Proto-Germanic *grabą, *grabō (“grave, trench, ditch”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrābʰ- (“to dig, scratch, scrape”). Related to graben (“to dig”). Compare Low German Graf, Graff, Dutch graf, English grave, Danish grav, Icelandic gröf, Serbo-Croatian grȍb (“grave”) and grȏblje (“graveyard, cemetery”), …

noun:Grad.tx: Borrowed from French grade (“a grade, degree”), from Latin gradus (“a step”).

noun:Gram.tx: From Middle High German gram (“displeasure, anger”), from Old High German *gramo, from Proto-Germanic *gramô (“anger”). Cognate with English grame. Akin also to Old Norse gramr (“wroth”) (whence the name of the sword), French and English chagrin.

noun:Gras.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gras, from Old High German gras, from Proto-West Germanic *gras, from Proto-Germanic *grasą, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“grow, become green”). Cognate with Danish græs, Dutch gras, English grass, and Low German Gras.

noun:Grippe.tx: Borrowed from French grippe (“influenza”), from gripper (“to seize, snatch”), from Frankish *grīpan, from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, whence German greifen. Eventually from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grab, to grasp”).

noun:Grund.tx: From Middle High German grunt, from Old High German grunt, from Proto-West Germanic *grundu, from Proto-Germanic *grunduz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰr̥mtu-. Cognate with West Frisian grûn, Dutch grond, English ground. Non-Germanic cognates include Albanian grundë (“brittle earth”) and gryej (“to erode, crumble”).

noun:Gruppe.tx: Borrowed from French groupe, from Italian gruppo, groppo, from Vulgar Latin *cruppus, (cf. Renaissance Latin grupus), from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz (“lump, group, body, crop”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewb- (“to crumple, bend, crawl”). Doublet of Kropf.

noun:Guru.tx: Borrowed from Hindi गुरु (guru) / Punjabi ਗੁਰੂ (gurū), from Sanskrit गुरु (guru, “venerable, respectable”).

noun:Gut.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German guot (“good”).

noun:Gymnasium.tx: Borrowed from Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).

noun:Graf.tx: Inherited from Middle High German grâve, from Old High German grāfio.

noun:Glühwürmchen.tx: From glühen (“to glow”) + Wurm (“worm”) + -chen (diminutive suffix) or Glühwurm + -chen.

noun:GAU.tx: Calque of English maximum credible accident.

noun:Gau.tx: From Middle High German göu, gou, from Old High German gawi, gouwi, from Proto-West Germanic *gawi, from Proto-Germanic *gawją from earlier *gaawja (“riverlands, lakeside land”), from collective *ga- + *awjō (“land by a waterway”). Cognates Cognate with Low German Gohe, Dutch gouw, West Frisian gea, goa, Old English ġē, German Aue.

noun:Gen.tx: Coined by Danish biologist Wilhelm Johannsen in 1909, from Ancient Greek γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”).

noun:Granate.tx: From Italian granata (“pomegranate”), from Latin grānum (“grain, seed”).

noun:Geschlechtsverkehr.tx: From Geschlecht + -s- + Verkehr. Compare Alemannic German Gschlächtsvercheer, Luxembourgish Geschlechtsverkéier.

noun:Geschlecht.tx: From Middle High German geslechte, from Old High German gislahti, a collective formation from slahta, from Proto-Germanic *slahtō, related to *slahaną (“to strike, hit”). Cognate with Dutch geslacht, Middle Low German geslechte, Italian schiatta, Polish szlachta. The Germanic root is that of Schlag, schlagen (“strike, beat”). The modern sense developed among this root's descendants first in …

noun:Gehacktes.tx: Nominalization of gehackt, past participle of hacken (“to chop”).

noun:Gebäude.tx: From Middle High German gebūwede, from the Old High German gibūidi (literally “that which has been built”), originally a collective noun to bauen. See there for more. By surface analysis, ge- + Bau + -de, related to bauen. Doublet of Gebäu. Cognate with Yiddish געבײַדע (gebayde)

noun:Gesicht.tx: From Middle High German gesiht, from Old High German gisiht, from Proto-West Germanic *gasihti. By surface analysis, ge- + Sicht. Cognate with Yiddish געזיכט (gezikht).

noun:Gestalt.tx: From Middle High German gestalt, the past participle of stellen (modern stellen, gestellt) used substantively. Cognates include Bavarian Gstoit and Yiddish געשטאַלט (geshtalt).

verb:gefallen.tx: From Middle High German gevallen, from Old High German gifallan. Equivalent to ge- (expressing the terminative aspect) + fallen.

verb:gewinnen.tx: From Middle High German gewinnen, winnen, from Old High German winnan, giwinnan, from Proto-West Germanic *winnan, from Proto-Germanic *winnaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, desire, love”). Cognate with Dutch winnen, Low German winnen, Old English ġewinnan, winnan (whence English win), Norwegian vinne, Swedish vinna.

noun:Gericht.tx: Related to gerecht. Cognate with Dutch gerecht.

noun:Grille.tx: From Middle High German grille, from Old High German grillo, probably from Latin gryllus (“grasshopper, cricket”), possibly onomatopoetic in origin, but perhaps borrowed in turn from Ancient Greek γρύλλος (grúllos, “Egyptian dance performer; painted caricature”), of unknown further origin.

noun:Gebet.tx: From Middle High German gebët, from Old High German gibet, from Proto-West Germanic *gabed.

noun:Gummi.tx: From Middle High German gummi (13th c.), from Medieval Latin gummi, byform of older cummi(s), which see.

prep:gegen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gegen, from Old High German gagan, from Proto-West Germanic *gagin, from Proto-Germanic *gagin. Cognate with Dutch tegen, English against, Icelandic gegn.

noun:Geschmack.tx: From Middle High German smac, from Old High German gismac, gismah, smac from Proto-West Germanic *smakku. Cognate with Dutch smaak, English smack, smatch, Swedish smak, Danish smag, Yiddish געשמאַק (geshmak).

noun:Gelatine.tx: Borrowed from French gélatine, from Italian gelatina, from Latin gelatus.

verb:gleiten.tx: From Middle High German glīten, from Old High German glītan, from Proto-West Germanic *glīdan, from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰleydʰ-. Compare Low German glieden, Dutch glijden, English glide.

noun:Gehirn.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gehirne, equivalent to ge- + Hirn.

adj:grau.tx: From Middle High German grā, from Old High German grāo, from Proto-West Germanic *grāu. Compare English gray, grey.

noun:Gehäuse.tx: From Late Middle High German gehiuse, geheus (15th c.), collective of Middle High German hūs (“house”).

prep:gen.tx: From Middle High German gēn, gein, from gegen with elision of intervocalic -g- (compare Getreide, Maid). Doublet of gegen (“against”). Cognate with Yiddish קיין (keyn).

noun:Großmutter.tx: From groß + Mutter. Displaced Middle High German eltermuoter, altermuoter (“grandmother”), related to English eldmother, eldermother.

verb:graben.tx: From Middle High German graben, from Old High German graban, from Proto-West Germanic *graban. Cognate with English grave (“to dig”), Polish grzebać (“to bury”), Czech hřésti (“to bury”). Doublet of gravieren. Compare German Grab (“grave”), Serbo-Croatian and Slovene grob (“grave”), Czech and Slovak hrob (“grave”), Polish grób (“grave”).

noun:Gebrüder.tx: From Middle High German gebruoder, gebrüeder, from Old High German gibruoder, equivalent to ge- + Bruder.

adj:gelb.tx: From Middle High German gel (inflected gelwe), from Old High German gelo, from Proto-West Germanic *gelu, from Proto-Germanic *gelwaz. The form gelb is derived from the Middle High German inflected stem (as in herb), while the variant gehl is from the uninflected stem and from dialects that reduce -lw- to -l- in all positions (as in fahl, kahl). It survives in set phrases. Cognate with Dutch …

noun:Gelegenheit.tx: From Middle High German gelegenheit. By surface analysis, gelegen + -heit.

adj:gerecht.tx: From Middle High German gereht, from Old High German gireht, from Proto-Germanic *garehtaz, from *ga- + *rehtaz. Compare Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (garaihts), Old English geriht, Dutch gerecht. Doublet of korrekt.

noun:Gesellschaft.tx: From Middle High German gesellescaft, from Old High German giselliscaft. Equivalent to Geselle + -schaft. Cognate with Dutch gezelschap.

noun:Gletscher.tx: Borrowed from Alemannic German Gletscher, from Romansh glatscher, from Vulgar Latin *glaciārium. First attested in the sixteenth century. Cognate with French glacier.

noun:Gott.tx: From Middle High German got, from Old High German got, from Proto-West Germanic *god, from Proto-Germanic *gudą. Compare Dutch god, English god, Danish gud, Gothic 𐌲𐌿𐌸 (guþ).

adj:glücklich.tx: From Glück + -lich. Cognate to Silesian East Central German glücklich, Low German glücklik (Paderbornisch) and Yiddish גליקלעך (gliklekh).

noun:Geschichte.tx: From Middle High German geschicht(e) (“event, struggle, story, history”), from Old High German gisciht, from the verb Proto-Germanic *skehaną, whence German geschehen. Unrelated to Schicht. Cognate with Bavarian Gschicht and Vilamovian gyśicht.

noun:Groschen.tx: From Middle High German grosse, from Medieval Latin (denarius) grossus (“thick (penny)”).

noun:Gasse.tx: From Middle High German gazze, from Old High German gazza, from Proto-West Germanic *gatwā, from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ. Compare Yiddish גאַס (gas).

verb:genießen.tx: From Middle High German genieȥen, from Old High German ginioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *ganeutan, equivalent to ge- + nießen. Akin to Dutch genieten, Yiddish געניסן (genisn).

verb:gießen.tx: From Middle High German gieȥen, from Old High German gioȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *geutan (“to pour”). Akin to Dutch gieten, Old Saxon giotan, Old English ġēotan, Old Norse gjóta (whence Danish gyde, Swedish gjuta), Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (giutan). Compare English gush. Further Indo-European cognates include Latin fundō (“to pour, to smelt”), Ancient Greek χέω (khéō, “to pour”) and Sanskrit जुहोति …

verb:grüßen.tx: From Middle High German grüeȥen from Old High German gruoȥen, gruoȥȥen, from Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan. Cognate with English greet, Old Saxon grōtian, Dutch groeten.

verb:gebrauchen.tx: Derived synchronically from ge- + brauchen, historically from Old High German gibrūhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *gabrūkan, compare Dutch gebruiken.

noun:Gebrauch.tx: Derived synchronically from gebrauchen, historically from Middle High German gebrūch, compare Dutch gebruik.

noun:Gebot.tx: From Middle High German gebot, from Old High German gibot. Compare Dutch gebod (“commandment”), Old English gebod (“order, command, mandate”).

noun:Geruch.tx: From Middle High German ruch from an original *rūk, compare Dutch reuk and Vilamovian gyruch.

verb:greifen.tx: From Middle High German grîfen, from Old High German grīfan, from Proto-West Germanic *grīpan, from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grab, grasp”).

adj:grob.tx: From Middle High German grob, grop, from Old High German grob, girob, of uncertain origin. Compare also Low German groff, Dutch grof, Saterland Frisian groaf, and English gruff. Per Kroonen, from Proto-West Germanic *grob, from Proto-Germanic *grubaz (“coarse”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewbʰ- (“to grind”). If so, then related to Old High German griobo (“twigs, kindling, firewood”), from …

noun:Gerste.tx: From Middle High German gërste, from Old High German gërsta, from Proto-West Germanic *gerstu (“barley”). Cognate with Dutch gerst.

noun:Gürtel.tx: From Middle High German gürtel, from Old High German gurtil, from Proto-West Germanic *gurdil, from Proto-Germanic *gurdilaz (“girdle, belt”). By surface analysis, gürten + el.

adv:gern.tx: From Middle High German gërne, from Old High German gërno, from Proto-West Germanic *gernō, from Proto-Germanic *gernô (“willingly, gladly”), an adverbial form of *gernaz (“eager, willing”). Akin to German Low German geren (Paderbornisch), Dutch gaarne, English yern, Swedish gärna, Danish gerne.

noun:Greis.tx: Inherited from Middle High German grīse, equivalent to a nominalization of the adjective greis, though shifted to strong inflection.

noun:Großvater.tx: From groß + Vater. Cognate to Dutch grootvader, German Low German Grautvader (Paderbornisch). Displaced Middle High German eltervater, altervater (“grandfather”). Compare English grandfather, which displaced English eldfather, elderfather in a similar manner.

noun:Getränk.tx: From Middle High German getrenke, a collective noun equivalent to ge- + Trank. Displaced Trank as the default word for “a drink" c. 1750. The spelling Getränk first attested c. 1650.

noun:Gebiet.tx: From Middle High German gebiet, gebiete (“jurisdiction; area of command”), from gebieten (“to command”). Compare Dutch gebied.

noun:Gewand.tx: From Middle High German gewant, from Old High German giwant, equivalent to ge- + winden.

noun:Gatte.tx: From Middle High German gate, from Old High German *gato, from Proto-West Germanic *gadō, from Proto-Germanic *gadô (“comrade”); related to Proto-West Germanic *gaduling (“relative, kinsman”). Akin to Old Saxon gigado, Old High German gatuling. Cognate to Dutch gegade, gade, English gad (“fellow, simpleton”).

noun:Gewehr.tx: From Middle High German gewer, from Old High German giwerida, equivalent to ge- + Wehr (“defense, resistance”), related to wehren. Cognate with Dutch geweer, Hunsrik Geweher.

noun:Grube.tx: From Middle High German gruobe, from Old High German gruoba, from Proto-Germanic *grōbō (“groove, furrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ-, whence also German graben (“to dig”). Cognate with Dutch groeve, English groove, Galician groba. Doublet of Groove.

noun:Guss.tx: From Middle High German guʒ, from Old High German guʒ, from Proto-West Germanic *guti, from the root of *geutan, whence German gießen (“to pour”). Cognate with Middle Low German gȫte (Swedish göt), Old English gyte.

noun:Größe.tx: From Middle High German grœze, from Old High German grōzī, from Proto-Germanic *grautį̄. Analysable as groß + -e.

noun:Geburt.tx: From Middle High German geburt, gepurt, from Old High German giburt, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gaburdiz, *gaburþiz, *burþiz. Cognate with Old English ġebyrd.

noun:Gespräch.tx: From Middle High German gespræche, gesprēche, from Old High German gisprāchi, from Proto-Germanic *gasprakją. Cognates with Low German Gespreek, Hunsrik Gesprech, Luxembourgish Gespréich, Dutch gesprek, Old English gesprecan.

noun:Galle.tx: From Middle High German galle, from Old High German galla, from Proto-West Germanic *gallā, from Proto-Germanic *gallǭ. Cognate with English gall.

noun:Galgen.tx: From Old High German galgo, from Proto-Germanic *galgô, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰalgʰ-, *ǵʰalg- (“long switch, rod, shaft, pole, perch”). Compare Dutch galg, English gallows, Danish galge.

noun:Garbe.tx: From Middle High German garbe, from Old High German garba, from Proto-West Germanic *garbā (“sheaf”).

noun:Garn.tx: From Middle High German garn, from Old High German garn, from Proto-West Germanic *garn.

noun:Gaumen.tx: From Middle High German gaume, from Old High German goumo, from Proto-Germanic *gaumô, alternative form of *gōmô (whence Old High German guomo).

noun:Gauner.tx: From thieves’ cant (Rotwelsch) Jauner, Joner (“gambler, cardsharp”), attested ca. 1500 alongside the verb jonen. Further usually derived from Yiddish יוון (Yoven/Yovon, “Greece”), from Hebrew יָוָן (yāwān), because Greeks were said to be skilful cardsharps (compare French Grec in this sense). The anlaut is due to hypercorrection based on the widespread Central German pronunciation of initial g- …

noun:Gedanke.tx: From Middle High German gedanc, from Old High German gidank. Compare Low German Gedank, Old English ġeþanc.

noun:Gefahr.tx: From Middle High German gevāre, gevære, from Old High German fāra, from Proto-Germanic *fērō. Cognate with English fear and Dutch gevaar.

noun:Gegend.tx: From Middle High German gegende, equivalent to gegen + -de, which is an alteration of older gegenōte, from Old High German geginōti, probably after Old French contree, whence also English country. Compare Dutch jegenode.

noun:Gegner.tx: From Middle Low German gēgenēre, which is derived from a verb gēgenen (“to face, encounter”). Compare German begegnen. Ultimately pertaining to gegen (“against”). Cognate to Dutch jegener (“opponent”). Compare English gainer.

noun:Geier.tx: From Middle High German gīr, from Old High German gīr.

noun:Gefäß.tx: From Middle High German gevǣȥe, from Old High German givāȥi; by surface analysis, ge- + fassen. Cognate with Plautdietsch Jefäss.

noun:Geige.tx: From Middle High German gīge, from Old High German gīga, of unclear origin. Possibly from a Proto-Germanic *gīganą (“to move, wish, desire”) (based on the movement of a violinist's arms), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeyǵʰ-, *ǵʰeygʰ-, an extension of *ǵʰeh₂- (“to yawn, gape, long for, desire”), though this is semantically dubious. Alternatively an independent onomatopoeic formation. Cognate with …

noun:Geisel.tx: From Middle High German gīsel, from Old High German gīsal, from Proto-West Germanic *gīsl, from Proto-Germanic *gīslaz.

noun:Geiß.tx: From Middle High German geiȥ, from Old High German geiȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *gait. Cognate with Dutch geit, English goat, Danish ged, Icelandic geit, Swedish get, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌹𐍄𐍃 (gaits); and with Latin haedus (“kid”).

noun:Geiz.tx: From late Middle High German gīze (“greed”), a back-formation from Middle High German gīzen, gītsen (“greedy”), from Middle High German gīt (“greed”), from Old High German *gītisōn, from Proto-West Germanic *gīdisōn. Cognate with Luxembourgish Gäiz and Old English ġītsian (“to desire, long for”).

noun:Gelenk.tx: From Middle High German gelenke (“joint, bend, waist”), from Old High German gilenki, gihlenki (“abdomen”), from Proto-Germanic *gahlankiją, from *hlankaz (“flexible, lank, slender”). Related to Middle High German lanke (“hip, flank, loin”), from Old High German hlanka (“side, flank, hip, loin”). Cognate with Hunsrik Gelenk.

noun:Gemüse.tx: From Middle High German gemüese, a derivative of Old High German muos (“food, victuals, porridge”), from Proto-Germanic *mōsą (“porridge, food”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“wet, fat, dripping”). By surface analysis, ge- + Mus + -e. Cognate to Bavarian Gmias, Pennsylvania German Gemies, Luxembourgish Geméis, and possibly English mush.

noun:Genosse.tx: From Middle High German genōȥ, from Old High German ginōȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *ganaut, from Proto-Germanic *ganautaz. The original etymological meaning was someone with whom enjoyment is shared, compare modern German genießen. Cognate with Dutch genoot.

noun:Gerücht.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gerüchte (Central German), borrowed from Middle Low German geruchte, gerüchte. This northern form replaced earlier Middle High German geruofte, gerüefte, from Old High German geruofti. The noun ultimately pertains to the verb rufen (“to call”) (Old High German ruofan, Old Saxon hrōpan). The Low German form is based on the shift -ft- → -cht- (cf. Nichte); the same …

noun:Geschoss.tx: From Middle High German geschoȥ, Old High German giscoȥ, derivation of the equivalent of schießen (“to shoot”), i.e. "that which is shot (a projectile)". The "floor, story" sense follows a semantic development "to shoot" > "to shoot up, go up quickly in height" > "levels of height" > "floor, story".

noun:Geselle.tx: From Middle High German geselle, from Old High German gisello, gisellio, from Proto-Germanic *gasaljô.

noun:Gesetz.tx: From Middle High German gesetze, gesetzede, from Old High German gisezzida (“fixing, determination, assessment”), from sezzen (“to make sit, set, put”), from Proto-West Germanic *sattjan (“to set, put down”).

noun:Gewalt.tx: From Middle High German gewalt, from Old High German giwalt, from Proto-West Germanic *gawald, from Proto-Germanic *gawaldą, from *ga- + *waldą (“power, authority”). Cognate with Yiddish געוואַלד (gevald), Dutch geweld, English wald.

noun:Gicht.tx: From Middle High German giht, from Old High German jiht, *giht, from Proto-Germanic *jihtiz.

noun:Giebel.tx: From Middle High German gibel, from Old High German gibil, from Proto-Germanic *gabla- (“top of a pitched roof”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰobʰ-lo-, likely derived from the stem *ǵʰebʰ-l-. Compare Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌻𐌰 (gibla), Old Norse gafl.

noun:Gier.tx: From Middle High German gir, from Old High German giri. The surname is from the noun, though it is also a Low German form of Geyer and in some personal name shortenings related to the ancient *gaiʀ (“spear”) as in Gerhardt.

noun:Gipfel.tx: From early modern (15th century) güpfel, diminutive of Middle High German gupf, gupfe (“highest point”), with further origin uncertain; perhaps related to German Kuppe. Cognate with Hunsrik Gippel, Vilamovian gejwuł. Compare Wipfel.

noun:Gitter.tx: From Middle High German geter n, umlauted as a collective or diminutive of gater m whence modern Gatter.

noun:Glanz.tx: From Middle High German glanz (noun and adjective), from Old High German glanz (adjective), from Proto-Germanic *glantaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰlond-o-, ultimately from the root *gʰlend-.

noun:Gleis.tx: The contemporary form is shortened from Geleise, from Middle High German geleis (“track”), cognate with Middle High German leise, from Old High German leisa, from Proto-Germanic *laisǭ (“track, trail”), from Proto-Indo-European *leys-eh₂-, from *leys- (“to trace, track”).

noun:Glied.tx: From Middle High German glit, gelit, from Old High German gilid, collective (with ge-) derivation from lid, from Proto-Germanic *liþuz. Cognate with Dutch lid, gelid, dialectal English lith. Also related with English limb.

noun:Glocke.tx: From Middle High German glocke, glogge, from Old High German klocca, from Late Latin clocca, probably of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (“bell”) (compare Welsh cloch, Irish clog), from Proto-Indo-European *klēg-, *klōg- (onomatopoeia). Cognate with Vilamovian głok and English clock.

noun:Glück.tx: From Middle High German gelücke (12th century), at first along the Lower and Middle Rhine. Probably borrowed from Old Dutch *gilukki as part of the Flemish knight culture; compare Middle Dutch gelucke (1240), whence modern Dutch geluk. (The fact that the word is attested in High German before Dutch must be disregarded in view of the minimal attestation of Old Dutch as a whole.) Further origin …

noun:Gnade.tx: From Middle High German gnāde, genāde, from Old High German gināda, reconstructible as Proto-West Germanic *ganāþu; o-construct of a verb attested only in Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌸𐌰𐌽 (niþan, “to help”), from Proto-Germanic *nēþō, from Proto-Indo-European *nēt-eh₂-. Compare Dutch genade, Old Saxon gināða, nāða.

noun:Gosse.tx: An originally only Central and Low German word. First High German attestation in early modern German as gossen (14th century). Pertaining to gießen (“to pour”). Cognate to Dutch goot.

noun:Grat.tx: Inherited from Middle High German grāt, from Old High German grāt, according to Pokorny, probably related to Proto-Germanic *granō (“awn”). Doublet of Gräte.

noun:Grenze.tx: Inherited from Middle High German grenize, borrowed from Old Polish granica, from Proto-Slavic *granica. By surface analysis, grań + -ica. The word spread westward in the 15th century and was reinforced by Luther’s Bible. Doublet of Granne.

noun:Grieche.tx: From Middle High German krieche, from Old High German Kriehha, from Proto-West Germanic *Krēkō (“Greeks”). Forms with initial k- are found in most old Germanic languages, though they seem to have lasted longer in High German than elsewhere.

noun:Gräte.tx: Inherited from Middle High German græte, the plural form of grāt, from Old High German grāt. Doublet of Grat, which see.

noun:Grieß.tx: From Middle High German griez, from Old High German grioz, from Proto-Germanic *greutą. Akin to Old Norse grjót, English grit.

noun:Griff.tx: From Middle High German grif, from Old High German grif, from Proto-West Germanic *gripi, from Proto-Germanic *gripiz.

noun:Groll.tx: From Middle High German grolle, related to English growl.

noun:Götze.tx: Attested from the 15th century, in the 14th in the compound götzenträger for "icon". In the 15th and 16th centuries a term for "cast image", and more generally for "image, likeness". In the 15th century used in the sense of "fool, stupid person", presumably influenced by Götz, a short form of the given name Gottfried. Grimm cites a folk song collected by Uhland (1881), based on a manuscript dated …

noun:Grütze.tx: From Middle High German grütze, from Old High German gruzzi (“coarse grains”), of the same root as Proto-Germanic *greutą = English grit, German Grieß. The term is applied to “ground” fruit because older desserts such as rote Grütze originally included cereal grains, and preserved the name despite substituting starch for the cereal grains; more recent dishes (e.g. gelbe Grütze) are named by …

noun:Gurke.tx: Borrowed from Old Polish ogórek, from Medieval Greek ἀγγούριον (angoúrion, “cucumber”). Cognate with Dutch augurk, English gherkin.

noun:Gärtner.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gartenære, gertenære, from Old High German gartināri; equivalent to Garten (“garden”) + -er (agent suffix).

adj:gesund.tx: From Middle High German gesunt, from Old High German gisunt, from Proto-West Germanic *gasund, a prefixed form of *sund, from Proto-Germanic *sundaz. Cognates include Bavarian gsund, Alemannic German gsund, Dutch gezond, English sound.

verb:gelingen.tx: From Middle High German gelingen, from Old High German gilingan, a prefixed form of lingan, from Proto-West Germanic *lingwan. Compare Yiddish געלינגען (gelingen).

noun:Glaube.tx: From Middle High German gloube, geloube, from Old High German giloubo, from Proto-West Germanic *galaubō, from Proto-Germanic *galaubô. More at glauben (“to believe”).

noun:Gewächs.tx: From Middle High German gewehse, variant of commoner gewahs. Collective formation from the root of wachsen (“to grow”). Compare Dutch gewas.

noun:Graben.tx: From Middle High German grabe, from Old High German grabo. The geological sense was introduced in 1888 by Austrian geologist Eduard Suess.

noun:Gefährte.tx: From Middle High German geverte, from Old High German giferto (“companion, he who travels with someone”), from Proto-West Germanic *gafardijō. By surface analysis, ge- + Fahrt + -e. Cognate with Old Dutch geferdi, Middle Low German gevērde. Also related with Old English ġefēra.

noun:Greif.tx: From Middle High German grīf, grīfe, from Old High German grīf, grīfo, borrowed from Latin gryphus. Early on associated with the unrelated verb in greifen (“to grab”); compare Middle Low German grīp. Possibly a doublet of Cherub.

noun:Güte.tx: From Middle High German güete, from Old High German guotī, from Proto-West Germanic *gōdī, from Proto-Germanic *gōdį̄; analysable as gut + -e.

verb:gähnen.tx: From Middle High German ginen, from Old High German ginēn, from Proto-West Germanic *gīnan.

verb:gären.tx: From Middle High German jësen, from Old High German jësan, from Proto-Germanic *jesaną. Variants with dissimilative hardening j- → g- before front vowels occur since Middle High German. The internal -r- is from the past forms (as in verlieren, schlagen), in part perhaps also from the causative Old High German jerien (“to make ferment”), from Proto-Germanic *jazjaną. These developments were …

verb:gebären.tx: From Middle High German gebërn, from Old High German gibëran, from Proto-West Germanic *gaberan, from Proto-Germanic *gaberaną. Cognate with English bear.

verb:gelten.tx: From Middle High German gëlten, from Old High German gëltan, from Proto-West Germanic *geldan, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną. Compare Dutch gelden, English yield, Icelandic gjalda.

adj:genau.tx: From Middle High German genoue, genouwe, geneuwe (“narrow, close, exact”), from ge- + nou(we) (“narrow, close, exact”), from Old High German *hnouw (“narrow, close”), from Proto-Germanic *hnawwaz. Cognate with Middle Low German nouwe, nau (“narrow, brief, exact”), Dutch nauw (“narrow, close”), Old English hnēaw (“niggardly, miserly, stingy”), Old Norse hnøggr (“niggardly, stingy, scant”).

adv:genau.tx: From Middle High German genoue, genouwe, geneuwe (“narrow, close, exact”), from ge- + nou(we) (“narrow, close, exact”), from Old High German *hnouw (“narrow, close”), from Proto-Germanic *hnawwaz. Cognate with Middle Low German nouwe, nau (“narrow, brief, exact”), Dutch nauw (“narrow, close”), Old English hnēaw (“niggardly, miserly, stingy”), Old Norse hnøggr (“niggardly, stingy, scant”).

verb:genesen.tx: From Middle High German genësen, from Old High German ginësan, from Proto-Germanic *ganesaną, from *nesaną.

det:genug.tx: From Middle High German genuoc, from Old High German ginuog, from Proto-West Germanic *ganōg, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz. Cognate with Dutch genoeg, Low German (ge)noog, English enough, West Frisian genôch, Danish nok, Swedish nog. Further Indo-European cognates: Latin nancīscor (“to get, to obtain”), Slovene nesti (“to carry”), Albanian kënaq (“to satisfy”).

pron:genug.tx: From Middle High German genuoc, from Old High German ginuog, from Proto-West Germanic *ganōg, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz. Cognate with Dutch genoeg, Low German (ge)noog, English enough, West Frisian genôch, Danish nok, Swedish nog. Further Indo-European cognates: Latin nancīscor (“to get, to obtain”), Slovene nesti (“to carry”), Albanian kënaq (“to satisfy”).

adv:genug.tx: From Middle High German genuoc, from Old High German ginuog, from Proto-West Germanic *ganōg, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz. Cognate with Dutch genoeg, Low German (ge)noog, English enough, West Frisian genôch, Danish nok, Swedish nog. Further Indo-European cognates: Latin nancīscor (“to get, to obtain”), Slovene nesti (“to carry”), Albanian kënaq (“to satisfy”).

adj:genug.tx: From Middle High German genuoc, from Old High German ginuog, from Proto-West Germanic *ganōg, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz. Cognate with Dutch genoeg, Low German (ge)noog, English enough, West Frisian genôch, Danish nok, Swedish nog. Further Indo-European cognates: Latin nancīscor (“to get, to obtain”), Slovene nesti (“to carry”), Albanian kënaq (“to satisfy”).

intj:genug.tx: From Middle High German genuoc, from Old High German ginuog, from Proto-West Germanic *ganōg, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz. Cognate with Dutch genoeg, Low German (ge)noog, English enough, West Frisian genôch, Danish nok, Swedish nog. Further Indo-European cognates: Latin nancīscor (“to get, to obtain”), Slovene nesti (“to carry”), Albanian kënaq (“to satisfy”).

adj:gerade.tx: From Middle High German gerat, from Old High German girat, equivalent to ge- + the root of Rad (“wheel”).

adv:gerade.tx: From Middle High German gerat, from Old High German girat, equivalent to ge- + the root of Rad (“wheel”).

noun:Gerät.tx: From Middle High German geræte (“consultation; equipment”), from Old High German girāti (“advice, consultation”), derived from rāt (“advice, council”). By surface analysis, ge- + Rat. The semantic development can, theoretically, be explained internally through a path “consultation” → “precaution” → “equipment”. However, the word has without doubt been influenced by another term, at hand in Old …

verb:gerben.tx: From Middle High German gerben, gerwen, garwen, from Old High German garawen, from Proto-West Germanic *garwijan. Related with gar (“cooked, ready”).

adj:gering.tx: From Middle High German geringe, from Old High German giringi, ringi (“low, plain, simple, light, easy”), from Proto-Germanic *ringwaz (“small, light, quick”), of uncertain origin, though possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wrengʷʰ- (“to squeeze, wring”) and cognate with Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, wring”), Ancient Greek ῥίμφα (rhímpha, “fast, quickly”). Cognate with Yiddish גרינג …

verb:geschehen.tx: From Middle High German geschehen, geschēn, geschegen, from Old High German giskehan, scehan, from Proto-West Germanic *skehan (“to spring, come up, emerge, happen”). Cognate to Bavarian gschehn and Dutch geschieden.

adj:glatt.tx: Inherited from Middle High German and Old High German glat, from Proto-West Germanic *glad.

verb:glühen.tx: From Middle High German glüejen, from Old High German gluoen. Compare Dutch gloeien, English glow, Danish glo.

verb:gönnen.tx: From Middle High German gunnen, from Old High German giunnan, from Proto-West Germanic *gaunnan (“to grant”), from *ga- + *unnan, from Proto-Germanic *unnaną (“to grant”). Cognate with Dutch gunnen, Yiddish גינען (ginen).

noun:Gunst.tx: From Middle High German gunst, from Old High German unst, from Proto-West Germanic *unsti. Cognate with Luxembourgish Gonscht, Dutch gunst, Swedish ynnest; related to the verb gönnen.

adj:günstig.tx: From Middle High German günstic, gunstic, equivalent to Gunst + -ig. Cognate with Middle Low German günstich.

adj:gültig.tx: From Middle High German gültic, from gülte, from gelten. Cognate with Low German güllig.

noun:Gemeinde.tx: From Middle High German gemeinde, from Old High German gemeinida, probably from Proto-Germanic (though the exact formations vary among and within the later languages), from *gamainiz (“shared, communal”) or *gamainijaną (“to share”) + *-iþō; specifically as gemein (“common”) + -de. Compare Old High German gimeinî, Hunsrik Gemeind, Luxembourgish Gemeng, Dutch gemeente, Old Saxon gimēntha …

noun:Gemeinschaft.tx: From gemein + -schaft. Cognate to German Low German Gemeenschopp (Gemeenschop), Middle Low German Gemeinschopp (in 16th century, used by Joachimus Magdeburgius).

noun:Göttin.tx: From Middle High German gotinne, from Old High German gutin, from Proto-West Germanic *gudinī, from Proto-Germanic *gudinī. Cognate with Dutch godin, Old English gyden, Swedish gudinna. By surface analysis, Gott + -in.

adj:geschickt.tx: From Middle High German geschicket (“arranged, prepared, ready, suitable”), synchronically analyzable as the past participle of schicken.

adv:geschickt.tx: From Middle High German geschicket (“arranged, prepared, ready, suitable”), synchronically analyzable as the past participle of schicken.

adv:gell.tx: Clipping of gelt es, from gelten (“to be valid”).

adj:galt.tx: From Middle High German galt. Compare Alemannic German galt (“not milch”), Cimbrian galt (“not milch”), Carinthian galt (“infertile or pregnant (therefore not milch)”), Swabian gall (“(of sheep) not pregnant”), German gelt (“infertile”), Tyrolean galt (“unfarmed land”), Danish gold (“barren; sterile; not milch”), Old Swedish galdvider (“barren tree”).

noun:Geologie.tx: From geo- + -logie, from New Latin geōlogia.

noun:Gemälde.tx: From Middle High German gemælde, gemælede, from Old High German gimālidi. Equivalent to ge- + malen + -de. Compare Middle Low German gemêlte, gemâlte.

adj:gewohnt.tx: From Middle High German gewonet (“customary”), past participle of gewonen, from Old High German giwonēn (“to get accustomed, bide, abide”). This verb has been displaced by reflexive sich gewöhnen, from related Middle High German gewenen (“to accustom, make accustomed”). Modern German gewohnt absorbed the related adjective gewohn (“common, usual”), from Proto-Germanic *gawunaz (whence Dutch …

noun:Gefecht.tx: From Middle High German gevëhte, from Old High German gifëht, from Proto-West Germanic *gafeht, from the verb *fehtaną (“to struggle with”). Equivalent to ge- + fechten. Cognate with Dutch gevecht, Old English ġefeoht.

noun:Götterdämmerung.tx: 18th century, from Götter (“gods”) + Dämmerung (“twilight”), a calque of Old Norse ragnarøkkr, an attested reinterpretation of ragnarǫk (literally “fate of the gods”). Popularised as the name of the last part of Richard Wagner's Ring cycle (1876).

verb:gekocht.tx: From Middle High German gekochet (past participle of kochen), from Old High German gikohhōt (past participle of kohhōn). The youth slang sense is a semantic borrowing from English cooked.

noun:Gegenwart.tx: From Middle High German gegenwart, from Old High German geginwartī, in which the component wart is cognate with Old High German werdan.

adj:giftig.tx: From Middle High German giftec; equivalent to Gift + -ig.

adv:giftig.tx: From Middle High German giftec; equivalent to Gift + -ig.

verb:gedenken.tx: From Middle High German gedenken, from Old High German gidenken, from Proto-West Germanic *gaþankijan. Equivalent to ge- + denken.

noun:Gros.tx: Borrowed from French gros (“great, large, thick”) (via Dutch), from Latin grossus.

verb:grauen.tx: From Middle High German grūwen, from Old High German (in)grūēn, probably from or related to Proto-West Germanic *grīsan (“to be frightened”).

adj:geheim.tx: From ge- + Heim (“home”); for the semantic development, compare heimlich and Dutch heimelijk (in contrast to English homely).

noun:Gobelin.tx: From a French manufacturing company, see above.

noun:Ganter.tx: From Low German Ganter, from a merger of Middle Low German gante and ganre, respectively from Proto-Germanic *ganutô and *ganzô. The former is cognate with Middle High German ganze (whence the southern Ganser), Dutch gent, English gannet. The latter is cognate with English gander.

noun:Gewürz.tx: From Middle High German gewürze, a collective of wurz (“wort, herb, root”), formed around the 14th century. Equivalent to ge- + Wurz. Compare Old High German giwurz f (“spice”) and English wort.

noun:Gespenst.tx: From Middle High German gespenst, gespenste, from Old High German gispensti (“temptation, (devilish) illusion”), from spanan (“to lure, to attract”), with ghosts interpreted as "illusions that lure one away"; see the related spannen (“to stretch, span”) for further etymology.

noun:Gepard.tx: Borrowed from French guépard, from Italian gattopardo (“ocelot, leopard”), from Latin cattus + pardus.

noun:Gürteltier.tx: Gürtel (“belt”) + Tier (“animal”). Displaced the earlier term Armadill (from Spanish armadillo), which had itself displaced Tatu (from Old Tupi).

noun:Geweih.tx: From Middle High German gewīge, *gewīhe (in hirzgewīh), ultimately: * a collective derivation from an Old High German *wīa (“branch”), related with Proto-Slavic *věja (compare Slovene veja), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *woh₁y-éh₂ (“branch, twig”), see also Sanskrit वया (vayā́, “branch, twig”). The consonants -g-, -h- are then mere hiatus breakers. * Alternatively a tool noun derived from …

noun:Glühbirne.tx: From glühen (“to glow”) + Birne (“pear”), due to the pear-like shape of (older) light bulbs.

noun:Getreide.tx: From Middle High German getreide, contracted from getregede, from late Old High German gitregidi (“produce, income”), a collective derived from tragen (“to bear; to bear fruit”) (DWDS).

noun:Grünspan.tx: From late Middle High German grüenspān, grüenspāt, a calque of Latin viride hispanicum (literally “Spanish green”) [from 15th c.]. By surface analysis, grün (“green”) + Span (“chip”), though this is a folk etymology.

noun:Gesetzesbrecher.tx: From Gesetz (“law”) + brechen (“to break”) + -er, literally “law breaker”.

noun:Geheimdienst.tx: Compound of geheim (“secret”) + Dienst (“service”), literally “secret service”.

adj:getrübt.tx: From Middle High German *getrüebet, from Old High German gitruobit, from Proto-West Germanic *drōbid, from Proto-Germanic *drōbidaz.

verb:gurgeln.tx: From Middle High German gurgeln, from Old High German gurgilōn, derived from gurgula, synchronically analyzed as Gurgel + -n.

verb:gilden.tx: From a colloquial merger of various dialectal forms of gelten and the related (obsolete) gülten. Compare for example Alemannic German gülte, gilde, Rhine Franconian gille, Central Franconian jelle, jölde.

verb:glänzen.tx: From Middle High German glenzen, from Old High German glanzen, from Proto-Germanic [Term?].

noun:Gewinn.tx: From Middle High German gewin, from Old High German giwin, from Proto-Germanic *gawinną. See gewinnen (“to win”).

adj:griechisch.tx: From Middle High German kriechisch, from Old High German chriehhisc. By surface analysis, Grieche + -isch.

verb:glimmen.tx: From Middle High German glimmen, from Proto-Germanic *glimmaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to gleam, shimmer, glow”). See also Norwegian glim, dialectal Old Swedish glim, glimma.

noun:Gleichgewicht.tx: gleich + Gewicht. Compare Norwegian Bokmål likevekt, Norwegian Nynorsk likevekt, Danish ligevægt.

verb:garen.tx: From gar (“cooked”), from Old High German garo (“prepared”). Not related to gären.

adj:gefangen.tx: From Middle High German gefangen, gevangen, from Old High German gifangan, from Proto-West Germanic *gafangan, past participle of *fą̄han, equivalent to ge- + fangen. Cognate with Middle Low German gevangen, Dutch gevangen.

noun:Gefängnis.tx: From Middle High German (ge)vancnisse, (ge)vencnisse (“capture, captivity”), since 15th century for the place of the captivity, equivalent to gefangen (“caught”) + -nis. More at fangen (“to catch”). Cognate with Dutch gevangenis.

noun:Geheimnis.tx: From geheim + -nis. Cognate to Dutch geheimenis (“secret”) and Yiddish געהיימעניש (geheymenish, “secret”).

noun:Grill.tx: Borrowed from English grill, itself from French gril.

adj:grausam.tx: From Middle High German grūsam, grūwesam. By surface analysis, grauen + -sam. Compare English gruesome, Danish grusom (“horrible”) and Dutch gruwzaam (“gruesome; cruel”). Related to ergrausen (“to frighten”).

adv:grausam.tx: From Middle High German grūsam, grūwesam. By surface analysis, grauen + -sam. Compare English gruesome, Danish grusom (“horrible”) and Dutch gruwzaam (“gruesome; cruel”). Related to ergrausen (“to frighten”).

noun:Geysir.tx: 19th century, from Icelandic Geysir, related to the verb geysa (“to gush”). See geyser for more.

noun:Geschirr.tx: From Middle High German geschirre (“harness, gear”), from Old High German giskirri, giscirri (literally “the trimmed (thing)”), from skeran (“to shear”), from Proto-Germanic *skeraną. Cognate with Alemannic German Geschirr.

noun:Geldbörse.tx: Borrowed from Dutch geldbeurs. Equivalent to Geld (“money”) + Börse (“purse, wallet”).

adv:gleichfalls.tx: From gleich + -falls. Earlier (des) gleichen Falls, equivalent to gleich + Fall + -s. Compare Middle Low German gelîkesvals, gelîkesvalles (> German Low German gliekfalls).

noun:Gebärmutter.tx: From gebären + Mutter. Compare Dutch baarmoeder.

noun:Geisterstadt.tx: Geister (“ghosts”) + Stadt (“town”); cognate with Luxembourgish Geeschterstad

noun:Geisterzug.tx: From Geist (“ghost”) + Zug (“train”). In the meaning "Cologne carnival parade", the second component is short for Umzug (“parade”).

noun:Gitarre.tx: Borrowed from Spanish guitarra. See also Zither.

adj:gewiss.tx: From Middle High German gewis, from Old High German giwis, from Proto-Germanic *gawissaz (“known, certain, sure”). Cognate with Dutch wis, English iwis.

adv:gewiss.tx: From Middle High German gewis, from Old High German giwis, from Proto-Germanic *gawissaz (“known, certain, sure”). Cognate with Dutch wis, English iwis.

noun:Gedankenexperiment.tx: From Gedanke + -n- + Experiment. Coined by Danish physicist and chemist Hans Christian Ørsted circa 1812.

adj:gemeinsam.tx: From Middle High German gemeinsam, from Old High German gimeinsam. Equivalent to gemein + -sam. Cognate with Dutch gemeenzaam.

adv:gemeinsam.tx: From Middle High German gemeinsam, from Old High German gimeinsam. Equivalent to gemein + -sam. Cognate with Dutch gemeenzaam.

noun:Gemeinplatz.tx: Calque of Latin locus commūnis, perhaps via English commonplace.

noun:Gottesdienst.tx: Analyzable as Gott (“God”) + -es- + Dienst (“service”). Inherited from Middle High German gotsdienst, from the Old High German genitive expression zi gotes thionōste, ultimately influenced by the usage of Ancient Greek λατρεία (latreía, “service, worship”) in the New Testament. Compare with Dutch godsdienst (“religion”), Danish gudstjeneste and Swedish gudstjänst (“service, worship”), …

verb:gaffen.tx: From Middle High German gaffen (“to gape; to stare”), from Old High German *gaffōn, from Proto-Germanic *gapōną (“to gaze, observe”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁y- (“to gape, be wide open”); influenced by and partly merged with Middle High German kaffen, a variant of kapfen (“to look, look surprised, gawk, wonder”), from Old High German kapfēn (“to look, stare, gawk, gape”), from Proto-West …

verb:grunzen.tx: From Middle High German grunzen, from Old High German grunzen, grunnezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *grunnattjan, from Proto-Germanic *grunnatjaną, cognate with English grunt.

noun:Glasur.tx: 16th century, derived from glasieren + -ur under influence of unrelated Lasur.

noun:Glatze.tx: From Middle High German glatz, from Old High German glaz (“braincase; weathered skull”). According to Duden and Pfeifer, derived from glatt (“smooth, sleek”), however with unexpected /ts/, perhaps from dialectal formation.

noun:Geschenk.tx: From Middle High German geschenke, equivalent to ge- + schenken.

noun:Gigantismus.tx: Gigant + -ismus. Compare French gigantisme, from Latin gigans (“giant”).

verb:genehmigen.tx: From genehm + -igen, 18th century, taking the place of earlier für genehm halten.

noun:Granit.tx: From Middle High German granīt, from Italian granito.

adj:geil.tx: From Middle High German geil, from Old High German geil, from Proto-West Germanic *gail ("wanton, lustful"), from Proto-Germanic *gailaz ("frothing, arrogant, tempestuous, violent, wanton").

noun:Gewitter.tx: From Middle High German gewiter, gewitere, from Old High German giwitiri, from Proto-West Germanic *gawidri, from Proto-Germanic *gawidriją, documented since the 9th century AD, equivalent to ge- + Wetter. Cognate with Hunsrik Gewitter. Distantly cognate in structure to English aweather.

noun:Gleichnis.tx: From Middle High German gelīchnisse, from Old High German gilīhnissi, gilīhnessi, from Proto-West Germanic *galīkanassī. Equivalent to gleich + -nis.

noun:Gedicht.tx: From Middle High German getiht, from tihten. See dichten for more.

adj:gemein.tx: From Middle High German gemein, from Old High German gimeini, from Proto-West Germanic *gamainī. Cognate with Old English gemǣne, English mean, Dutch gemeen, Danish gemen, Swedish gemen and Norwegian gemen.

adv:gemein.tx: From Middle High German gemein, from Old High German gimeini, from Proto-West Germanic *gamainī. Cognate with Old English gemǣne, English mean, Dutch gemeen, Danish gemen, Swedish gemen and Norwegian gemen.

noun:Gämse.tx: From Middle High German gemeze, from Old High German gamiza (form only attested in a 13th-century manuscript). The variant Gams f is from Middle High German gamz m, f, n, from Old High German *gamuz or *gamaz (probably a masculine or neuter). These forms can be derived from Vulgar Latin *camōcius m, *camōcia f, which also underlie most of the dialectal Romance forms in Switzerland and northern …

adj:geschwind.tx: From Middle High German swinde, from Old High German *swind, from Proto-West Germanic *swinþ. See English swith.

noun:Gestank.tx: From Middle High German gestanc, from Old High German gistank.

noun:Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung.tx: From Geschwindigkeit (“speed, pace, velocity”) + -s- + Begrenzung (“limit, demarcation”).

noun:Gummizelle.tx: From Gummi (“rubber, gum”) + Zelle (“cell, small room”).

noun:Gezeiten.tx: From the plural of Middle High German gezīt (“particular time, such as a feast or prayer time”), from Old High German gizit (“passage of time”), from gi- + zit. The modern sense is loaned from cognate Middle Low German getīde, whence also Tide. Related to Zeit.

noun:Gießkanne.tx: Compound of gießen (“to pour, to water”) + Kanne (“can, pot”)

noun:Genom.tx: Coined by German botanist Hans Winkler in 1920 as a blend of Gen (“gene”) + Chromosom (“chromosome”).

noun:Gips.tx: From Middle High German gips, from late Old High German gips, from Proto-West Germanic *gips.

noun:Grammatik.tx: From Middle High German grāmatic, grāmaticā, from Old High German grammatih, gramatih, borrowed from Latin (ars) grammatica, from Ancient Greek γραμματικὴ τέχνη (grammatikḕ tékhnē, “art of letters”).

adj:grammatikalisch.tx: From Latin grammaticalis. Analysable as Grammatik + -al + -isch.

noun:Gehör.tx: From Middle High German gehœre, from Old High German *gihōra (attested as acc. sg. kehorun). Equivalent to ge- + hören; compare Dutch gehoor. This was a less common byform of Middle High German gehœrde, from Old High German gihōrida, itself cognate with Old Dutch *gehōrtha (attested as gehortoir, error for dat. sg. gehorton) and Old Saxon gihōritha. All of these words were originally feminines, …

noun:Geräusch.tx: From Middle High German geriusche, from Middle High German rūschen, riuschen, from (unattested) Old High German *rūskōn, from Proto-Germanic *rūskōną (“to make noise”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Hrews-, *HrewH- (“to move, drive, agitate”); equivalent to ge- + rausch(en) (“to rustle”).

noun:Gackern.tx: See gackern (“sound made by a hen”)

noun:Geduld.tx: From Middle High German gedult, from Old High German gidult, githult (8th century), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *þuldi. Related to Dutch geduld, Vilamovian gydułd, English thild and thole. See dulden for more.

noun:Gottheit.tx: From Middle High German gotheit, from Old High German gotheit, goteheit, equivalent to Gott + -heit. Compare English godhead, Dutch godheid.

noun:Gewölbe.tx: From Middle High German gewelbe, from Old High German giwelbi, from Proto-Germanic *hwalbiją (“arch; vault; ceiling”). Cognate with Old English hwealf (“arched or vaulted covering”).

adj:geduldig.tx: From Middle High German gedultic, from Old High German gidultig; By surface analysis, Geduld + -ig. Cognates include Dutch geduldig and Old English geþyldig.

noun:Gebirge.tx: From Middle High German gebirge, from Old High German gibirgi; originally a collective noun equivalent to ge- + Berg.

noun:Granatapfel.tx: From Middle High German grānātapfel, a partial calque of Latin malum/pomum granatum (literally “seedy apple”). Secondarily analysable as Granate (“grenade”) + Apfel (“apple”); see the former.

noun:Gewissen.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German giwizzani, a calque of cōnscientia; equivalent to ge- + wissen.

noun:Galerie.tx: From the earlier form Gallerei, from Italian galleria. Compare French galerie.

noun:Gesäß.tx: From Middle High German gesæȥe, geseȥȥe, gesetze, gesōȥe, from Old High German gisāȥi (“seat, residence, camp, backside”), from "where one sits on"; compare German sitzen. Possibly ultimately from a Proto-Germanic *sētiją. Compare also English seat, Icelandic sæti, Middle Dutch gesaete.

noun:Geldwechsler.tx: Geld (“money”) + wechseln (“to change/exchange”) + -er or Geld + Wechsler.

noun:Gebiss.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?].

noun:Gepäck.tx: From Late Middle High German gepac, synchronically analyzable as a collective nominal formation from Pack (“package, bundle”) (DWDS).

verb:garnieren.tx: Eventually from Old French guarnir, from Frankish *warnijan (“to ward, take care of”), from Proto-Germanic *warnijaną. Related to but not identical with German warnen, English warn. Perhaps partly through Middle Low German garnēren (“to clad with wood”, 15th c.), but in the contemporary sense (17th c.) directly from modern French garnir.

adj:generös.tx: From French généreux, from Middle French genereux, from Latin generōsus, from genus (“birth, origin”) + -ōsus.

adj:gierig.tx: From Middle High German giric, girich, from Old High German girīg, gerag, from Proto-West Germanic *girīg, *gerag, from Proto-Germanic *girigaz, *geragaz, later variants of *gerugaz. By surface analysis, Gier + -ig.

noun:Gefallen.tx: From earlier Gefalle, from Middle High German geval, equivalent to a deverbal of gefallen (compare Fall). Originally a strong noun, but seemingly shifting to a weak paradigm before regularizing back into its modern, strong form by adapting the oblique weak ending in the nominative. Grimm notes inconsistent gender usage between masculine and neuter under the influence of etymology 2, including in …

adj:getreu.tx: From Middle High German getriuwe, from Old High German [Term?].

prep:getreu.tx: From Middle High German getriuwe, from Old High German [Term?].

noun:Geschäft.tx: From Middle High German gescheft, from Old High German giscaft, from Proto-West Germanic *gaskafti. Cognate with Yiddish געשעפֿט (gesheft).

noun:Gewohnheit.tx: From Middle High German gewonheit, from Old High German giwonaheit. Equivalent to gewohn + -heit, the former being an obsolete variant of gewohnt. Compare gewöhnlich.

noun:Gebühr.tx: From Middle High German gebür(e), from Old High German giburi. Deverbal from gebühren.

noun:Göre.tx: From German Low German Gör, Göre (17th century). A relation with English girl, likewise of uncertain origin, is probable.

noun:Gaspedal.tx: Gas (“gas”) + Pedal (“pedal”). Gas, which does not mean “petrol” in German, refers to the fuel-air mixture in the engine, which is regulated by the throttle.

adj:geizig.tx: Alteration (due to German Geiz) of Middle High German gītic, gītich, gītec, from Old High German gītag, equivalent to Geiz + -ig. Doublet of geitig.

noun:Gehalt.tx: From Middle High German gehalt, deverbal from gehalten (“to keep still, retain, preserve, imprison”), itself from halten (“to hold”). The earliest attested sense of the noun is “custody, prison”. In some southern dialects it also means “room, container, closet”. The modern sense develops in the 15th century, at first in the context of coins and metal alloys.

adj:galaktisch.tx: From Ancient Greek γᾰ́λᾰκτ- (gắlăkt-, “milk”) + -isch, after Galaxie.

noun:Gruft.tx: From Middle High German gruft, kruft, from Old High German gruft, kruft, chruft, from Proto-West Germanic *krufti, an early borrowing from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ). Cognate with Dutch krocht, Middle Low German kruft, Old English cruft. Doublet of Grotte and Krypta. Some authors think that the word may have been merged with a native West Germanic *grufti, deverbal from …

noun:Gehirnwäsche.tx: From Gehirn + Wäsche. Calque of English brainwash, itself a calque of Chinese 洗腦 /洗脑 (xǐnǎo).

verb:grenzen.tx: From Middle High German grenizen. By surface analysis, Grenze + -en.

verb:geleiten.tx: From Middle High German geleiten, from Old High German gileitan, gileiten, from Proto-Germanic *galaidijaną, equivalent to ge- + leiten. Compare with English belead.

verb:genieren.tx: From French gêner + -ieren. First attested in the 18th century.

adj:gütlich.tx: From Middle High German guotlīch, from Old High German guotlīh, from Proto-West Germanic *gōdalīk, from Proto-Germanic *gōdalīkaz. By surface analysis, gut + -lich.

adj:gemäß.tx: From messen. Cognate to Old English ġemǣte (whence English meet).

prep:gemäß.tx: From messen. Cognate to Old English ġemǣte (whence English meet).

adv:gewissermaßen.tx: From gewisser Maßen, which has a genitival relict of Middle High German māȥe f; by surface analysis, gewiss + -er- + -maßen.

noun:Gedächtnis.tx: From Middle High German gedæhtnisse, gedæhtnüsse, from Old High German githehtnissī. By surface analysis, gedacht + -nis. Cognate with Dutch gedachtenis.

noun:Garnele.tx: Borrowed from Dutch garnaal, earlier also garneel. Further origin unknown.

noun:Gesang.tx: From Middle High German gesanc, from Old High German [Term?]. By Surface analysis ge- + singen.

adj:garstig.tx: From Middle High German garst, from Old High German garst (“foul taste”), of uncertain origin. -ig Kluge compares Latin fastidium (“disgust, loathing”) or horridus (“rude, rough”), while Pokorny suggests a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”).

noun:Gaukler.tx: From Middle High German goukelære, gougelære, gouchelære, koukelære, from Old High German gougalāri, goukalāri. Related to Middle Low German gȫkelere, Old English ġēogolere, Old Norse kuklari.

verb:geraten.tx: From Middle High German gerāten, from Old High German girātan (“to counsel, decide, turn towards, take care of”), from Proto-West Germanic *garādan, from Proto-Germanic *garēdaną (“to have a plan for, take forethought of, purpose, intend, aim at”), equivalent to ge- + raten. Cognate with Middle Low German gerâden, Dutch geraden (“to form an assumption, guess”), Middle English ireden (“to counsel, …

adj:geraten.tx: From Middle High German gerāten, equivalent to ge- + raten. Cognate with Middle Low German gerâden. See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Gimpel.tx: Unrounded from Late Middle High German gümpel (15th c. in Tyrol). Plausibly from Middle High German gumpen (“to jump, hop, skip, bounce”), itself of uncertain origin.

noun:Gnadenstoß.tx: From Gnade (“grace, mercy”) + -n- + Stoß (“push, shove, bump”).

noun:Geisterfahrer.tx: Geist (“ghost”) + Fahrer (“driver”). Compare Dutch spookrijder and Swedish spökförare.

verb:grünen.tx: From Middle High German grüenen, grūnen, gruonen, from Old High German gruonēn, from Proto-West Germanic *grōnijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōnijaną.

verb:gedeihen.tx: From Middle High German gedīhen, from Old High German githīhan, from Proto-West Germanic *gaþį̄han, from Proto-Germanic *gaþinhaną; cognates include Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌸𐌴𐌹𐌷𐌰𐌽 (gaþeihan), Dutch gedijen. A prefixed variant of Middle High German dīhen, from Old High German thīhan, from Proto-West Germanic *þį̄han, from Proto-Germanic *þinhaną. Compare with obsolete English thee (“to thrive”).

verb:gleichen.tx: From Middle High German gelīchen, from Old High German gilīhhon, from Proto-Germanic *galīkōną.

phrase:geschehen ist geschehen.tx: Literally, “happened is happened”. Compare the English snowclone X is X.

noun:Gegensatz.tx: From gegen- + Satz (“set”). Calque of Latin oppositio.

noun:Grotte.tx: From Italian grotto, from Vulgar Latin grupta, from Classical Latin crypta. Doublet of Krypta.

conj:geschweige.tx: First-person singular indicative present of geschweigen (“to be silent”) (from Middle High German geswîgen, from Old High German giswîgên), which has been obsolete at least since the 18th century.

adj:geistreich.tx: From Middle High German geistrīch, equivalent to Geist + -reich. Cognate to Dutch geestrijk.

adj:gehorsam.tx: From Middle High German gehōrsam, from Old High German gihōrsam, from Proto-West Germanic *gahauʀisam.

noun:Geschwür.tx: From Middle High German geswër (“abscess”). Related to Russian хворь.

noun:Germane.tx: From Latin Germanus, used to designate related peoples of central and northern Europe.

noun:Gefährt.tx: From Middle High German geverte (“way, ride, walk, behaviour”), from Old High German *giferti (attested as giverte, etc.), from faran, whence modern fahren. The contemporary sense (17th c.) after cognate Middle Low German gevērde.

verb:grausen.tx: From Middle High German grūsen, from Old High German (ir)grū(wi)sōn, from the root of grauen (“dread, horror”).

adj:geborgen.tx: From Middle High German geborgen, from Old High German giborgan.

adj:gestrig.tx: From Middle High German gesteric, from Old High German gesterīg. By surface analysis, gestern + -ig.

noun:Gugelhupf.tx: From Gugel, a kind of pointed hood, from Latin cucullus. The origin of the second element is debated.

adv:größtenteils.tx: Univerbation of größten + Teils, adverbial genitive of größter Teil.

verb:googeln.tx: From Google + -n or English google (verb) + -n. The sequence -le- was respelt -el- to allow for regular German conjugation.

noun:Geflügel.tx: Inherited from Old High German gifugili. The expected modern form is *Gefügel, a collective form pertaining to Vogel (“bird”), cf. similar Dutch gevogelte. The connection with Vogel was lost in German and the word was at some point re-interpreted as Geflügel, that is “creatures with wings; winged ones”. Cf. Flügel (“wing”).

noun:Gürtelrose.tx: Gürtel (“belt”) + Rose (“rose”), from the beltlike shape and red color of the rash.

adj:grammatisch.tx: From Latin grammaticus, from Ancient Greek γραμματικός (grammatikós). Analysable as Grammatik + -isch.

adj:gesamt.tx: From Middle High German gesamt, gesament, from Old High German gisamanōt, from samanōn (“to gather, collect”), from Proto-West Germanic *samnōn, from Proto-Germanic *samnōną (“to bring together”).

noun:Guinee.tx: Borrowed from French guinée, from English guinea.

noun:Gewebe.tx: A deverbal noun from weben (“to weave”). Cognate with Hunsrik Geweb.

noun:Gangrän.tx: Borrowed from French gangrène, from Latin gangraena, from Ancient Greek γάγγραινα (gángraina, “gangrene”), from Ancient Greek γράω (gráō, “to gnaw”).

adj:gelegen.tx: From Middle High German gelegen, from Old High German gelegan, gilegan; from liegen.

adj:germanisch.tx: From Latin Germanicus + -isch; equivalent to Germane + -isch.

verb:grinsen.tx: Intensive form of Middle High German grinnen, probably ultimately from the root of greinen (“to moan, whine”).

verb:gieren.tx: From Middle High German or Middle Low German gīren (“to open one’s jaws, gape, scream”), from Proto-Germanic *gīran- and ultimately imitative. Cognate with Dutch gieren (“to scream”). Related also with German Geier (“vulture”) and gähnen, English yawn. In standard German, the word has always been associated with unrelated Gier (“greed, lust”) and is typically regarded a derivative thereof. Also …

noun:Gewähr.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?].

adj:gewieft.tx: Probably past participle from Middle High German wīfen (“to wind, swing”), related to Wipfel.

noun:Gestade.tx: From Middle High German gestade, gestat, from Old High German stad, stado, from Proto-Germanic *staþaz. Cognate with English stathe and Bavarian Gstättn (see also Gstätten).

noun:Gurt.tx: From Middle High German gurt, a backformation from the verb gürten (“to gird”) and the noun gürtel (“belt”). See modern German gürten and Gürtel for more.

adv:gemach.tx: From Middle High German gemach, from Old High German gimah (“calm, comfortable”), from Proto-West Germanic *gamak, related to the root of machen (“to do, carry out”).

intj:gemach.tx: From Middle High German gemach, from Old High German gimah (“calm, comfortable”), from Proto-West Germanic *gamak, related to the root of machen (“to do, carry out”).

noun:Ganja.tx: Borrowed from English ganja, from Hindi गांजा (gāñjā).

noun:Goi.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish גוי (goy, “Gentile”), from Hebrew גּוֹי (gói, “nation”).

noun:Großfürst.tx: From groß (“big, great”) + Fürst (“prince”, viz. generic and as ruler's title).

noun:Gesinde.tx: From Middle High German gesinde, from Old High German gasindi, gisindi, gisindo, from Proto-Germanic *gasinþiją, from the root *senþ-, sinþ- "to go, travel; seek, aim", from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”). More at sīþ, *sandijaną. A neuter collective to the masculine gasint (archaic modern German Gesind (“wayfellow, fellow traveller; follower”)). Cognate with Old English ġesīþ, …

verb:gucken.tx: From Middle High German gücken, guggen (“to look inquisitively, peek, peer”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a specialised use of Middle High German gücken, gucken (“to cuckoo, call or cry like a cuckoo”), from Old High German guckōn, gukkōn (“to cuckoo”). The pronunciation (and spelling) with k- is commonly explained as an influence of German Low German kieken (from Middle Low German kîken). …

verb:genügen.tx: From Middle High German genüegen, from Old High German ginuogen, from Proto-West Germanic *ganōgijan, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgijaną, from the adjective Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz (“enough, sufficient”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₂nóḱe (“he has reached, attained”), perfective of *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”). Cognate with Dutch genoegen, Icelandic nægja and Norwegian Nynorsk nøye.

noun:Gebäck.tx: From Middle High German gebac, from Old High German *gibak, *gibah, from Proto-West Germanic *gabak (“something baked, pastry”), collective form of *bak, from Proto-Germanic *baką (“baked goods, baking”). Cognate with Middle Low German gebak (whence German Low German Gebäck), Dutch gebak, Old English ġebæc. More at English batch.

noun:Geschwister.tx: From Middle High German geswister, from Old High German giswëstar, equivalent to ge- + Schwester. Compare Old Saxon gisustrōni (“sibling”), Old Frisian swesterne, susterne, sisterne (“siblings”), Old English ġesweostren (“maternal cousin, sister”).

adj:gehörnt.tx: From Middle High German gehürnet, from Old High German *gihurnit, from Proto-Germanic *hurnidaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *hurnijaną (“to horn”), equivalent to ge + Horn + -t. Cognate with Old Frisian herned (“horned”), Old English ġehyrned (“horned”) (English horned), Old Norse hyrndr (“horned”).

noun:Gardine.tx: From early modern Dutch gardine (contemporary Dutch gordijn), from French courtine, from Old French cortine, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”).

verb:gründen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gründen. Analyzable as Grund + -en with derivational umlaut.

noun:Gegenstand.tx: gegen- + Stand. Calque of Latin obiectum; whereas subiectum has been calqued with Unterstand but this is now only used, at best, by philosophers.

noun:Gerüst.tx: From Middle High German gerüste, from Old High German girusta.

verb:glücken.tx: From Middle High German gelücken, derived from gelücke (“luck, success”), whence modern Glück.

phrase:Gott mit uns.tx: Interpretation of Biblical Hebrew עִמָּנוּאֵל ('imanu'éll) (Isaiah 7:14, 8:10) and Koine Greek μεθ’ ἡμῶν ὁ Θεός (meth’ hēmôn ho Theós) (Matthew 1:23). Compare Russian с на́ми Бог (s námi Bog).

noun:Gesprächspartner.tx: Gespräch (“conversation”) + -s- + Partner (“partner”). Cognate with Dutch gesprekspartner.

noun:Geißel.tx: From Middle High German geisel(e), from Old High German geisila (“whip”). Cognate with Dutch gesel. The spelling with -ß- reflects sporadic devoicing; compare the frequent pronunciations of niesen or Preiselbeere. Its use for distinguishing between Geißel and Geisel (“hostage”) is an arbitrary convention, which fully established itself only around 1900. (The two words are not related but became …

verb:gravieren.tx: Early 18th century. Either directly from modern French graver or through Dutch and Middle Dutch graveren (13th c.), from Old French graver, from Frankish *graban, from Proto-Germanic *grabaną. Doublet of graben.

adj:gravierend.tx: Participle of Middle High German gravieren (“to burden”), from Latin gravāre, gravō (“to burden”), from gravis (“heavy”).

adj:gängig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gengec, displacing earlier Middle High German genge (which survives in gang und gäbe). By surface analysis, Gang + -ig.

noun:Glotze.tx: Derived from the colloquial term glotzen (“to stare”).

verb:glotzen.tx: From Middle High German glotzen, from Old High German *glozzōn, from Proto-West Germanic *glotōn. Cognate with Old Norse glotta, English gloat.

adj:gesprächig.tx: From Middle High German gespræchec, from Old High German gisprāhhīg. By surface analysis, Gespräch + -ig.

adv:gegebenenfalls.tx: Univerbation of gegebenen (“given”) + Falls (“case”), originally an adverbial genitive. Compare andernfalls.

adv:gleichsam.tx: 15th century, from gleich + -sam. Earlier attested as a Middle High German noun gelīchsame (“image, double, likeness”) and a verb gelīchsamen (“to compare”); and Old High German gilīhsam (“similar, hypocrite”).

adj:gleichschenklig.tx: gleich (“equal”) + Schenkel (“leg”) + -ig; calque of Ancient Greek ἰσοσκελής (isoskelḗs, literally “equal-legged”)
