adj:greis.tx: From Middle High German grīs, from Old High German grīs, from Proto-West Germanic *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz (“grey”). Doublet of regional gries (“grey”). Also cognate with Dutch grijs, French gris.

noun:Gelübde.tx: From Middle High German gelübede, from Old High German gilubida. Related to verb geloben (“to vow, to make an oath”), and cognate to Dutch gelofte (“vow”).

verb:geloben.tx: From Middle High German geloben, from Old High German gilobōn, from Proto-West Germanic *galobōn, equivalent to ge- + loben. Cognate to Low German gelowen, Old English ġelofian.

adj:gehalten.tx: From Middle High German gehalten, from Old High German gihaltan.

verb:gelangen.tx: From Middle High German gelangen, from Old High German gilangōn, synchronically analyzed as an ablaut formation from gelingen (“to succeed”) (Duden).

noun:Gebüsch.tx: From Late Middle High German gebüsche. By surface analysis, ge- + Busch.

adj:geschmeidig.tx: From Middle High German gesmīdec (“easy to forge or work”), related to schmieden.

noun:Gelände.tx: From Middle High German gelende, from Old High German gilenti; originally a collective noun equivalent to ge- + Land.

adj:gewaltig.tx: From Middle High German gewaltec, from Old High German giwaltīg, equivalent to Gewalt + -ig. Compare Middle Low German weldich, whence Swedish väldig (“huge”).

noun:Gemach.tx: From Middle High German gemach, from Old High German gimah. Equivalent to a nominalization of gemach, originally an adjective meaning "comfortable, suitable".

noun:Gutes.tx: Nominalization of gut (“good”). Compare Silesian East Central German Guttes n, Alemannic German Guets n.

verb:gewähren.tx: From Middle High German (ge)wern, from Old High German (gi)werēn, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *warjan (“to defend, ward off”). Compare English guarantee and warrant.

noun:Glucke.tx: From Middle High German klucke, derived from the verb klucken (“to cluck”), from Proto-Germanic *klukkwōną, of onomatopoeic origin. The g- by dissimilation.

noun:Gestein.tx: From Middle High German gesteine, from Old High German gisteini, a collective formation equivalent to ge- + Stein. Compare Dutch gesteente.

adj:grimmig.tx: Middle High German grimmec, from Old High German grimmīg, grim; see Grimm (“rage, wrath”). Cognate with English grim.

noun:Ganzes.tx: Noun formed from the adjective ganz (“whole, entire”).

verb:grämen.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German grem(m)en, ultimately from the root of gram (“angry”).

adj:gespalten.tx: From Middle High German gespalten, from Old High German gispaltan. Equivalent to ge- + spalten.

adj:gütig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German güetec. By surface analysis, Güte (“kindness”) + -ig. Cognate with Dutch goedig.

noun:Gehege.tx: From Middle High German gehege, from Old High German gahagi, from Old High German Hag, from Proto-West Germanic *hagō.

noun:Gestirn.tx: From Middle High German gestirn, gestirne, from Old High German gistirni. By surface analysis, ge- (collective prefix) + Stern (“star”).

noun:Griffel.tx: From Middle High German griffel, from Old High German griffil. By surface analysis, Griff + -el.

noun:Gral.tx: From Middle High German grāl, from Old French graal, from Latin gradalis.

adj:gries.tx: From German Low German, from Middle Low German grîs, from Old Saxon grīs, from Proto-West Germanic *grīs (“grey”). Doublet of greis (“aged, grey-haired”) and Greis (“old man”).

noun:Geck.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German geck (“fool”). The same word has later been borrowed again from Ripuarian as jeck (“crazy”) and Jeck (“fool; carnival reveler”).

intj:gluck.tx: Of imitative origin (lautmalend), see also glucken (“to cluck; to chug a liquid”).

noun:Gefreiter.tx: Nominalized past participle of freien in the obsolete meaning “to make free, to exempt from duty”. From the fact that the rank was originally freed from sentry duty.

adj:gescheit.tx: From Middle High German geschīde (“sensible, sly”), derived from schīden. Related to scheiden (“to separate, distinguish”). Based on the notion of “prudent, circumspect” it was associated with scheuen (“to shun, shy away”) and therefore frequently spelt gescheut. The -t thence and through generalisation of final devoicing. Cognate with Vilamovian gysiajt, Bavarian gscheid, and Swabian gscheid.

noun:Granat.tx: From Middle High German grānāt which was borrowed from Medieval Latin granatus, most likely a substantivized masculine form of *lapis granatus.. More at Granatapfel. The term Granat in the sense of shrimp was borrowed from Middle Low German garner, garnat or garnol, itself borrowed from Middle Dutch grenat (as spoken in Flanders).

noun:G-Punkt.tx: Calque of English G-spot, named after German physician and scientist Ernst Gräfenberg (1881–1957).

intj:geschenkt.tx: The interjection is to be understood as “I cancel whatever moral debt there may be”.

adj:gelehrt.tx: From Middle High German gelērt, gelēret, from Old High German gilērit.

adj:gedrungen.tx: From Middle High German gedrungen, from Old High German gidrungan.

verb:gewärtigen.tx: From the adjective gewärtig. From Middle High German gewęrtec.

noun:Gneis.tx: From Middle High German gneist (“spark”), from Old High German gneisto (“spark”), from Proto-West Germanic *gahnaistō, perhaps from the ultimate source of knistern (“to crackle”).

noun:Graus.tx: From Middle High German grūs, grūse. Synchronically from grausen.

adj:gruselig.tx: From gruseln (“to provoke fear”) + -ig. Compare English gruesome.

noun:Geleit.tx: Deverbal noun from geleiten. Compare English belead.

noun:Gemüt.tx: From Middle High German gemüete, from Old High German gimuati. Analyzable as ge- + Mut. Cognate with Dutch gemoed, Old English gemēde.

noun:Grashüpfer.tx: From Gras (“grass”) + Hüpfer (“hopper”). A chiefly northern word, partly from Middle Low German grashüppel (and variants). Not attested in continental West Germanic before the 16th century, but considering Old English græshoppa perhaps older. Compare the similar motivation in German Heuschrecke.

adj:grell.tx: From Middle High German grel (“angry, violent”), a derivative of grellen (“to cry loudly, scream”). More at grill.

adj:grantig.tx: Uncertain. Kluge and Pfeifer put forward a possible relation to greinen (“to cry, whine”).

verb:gestatten.tx: From Middle High German gestaten, Old High German gistatōn, related to Status (“status”); see there for more.

verb:grollen.tx: From Middle High German grollen (“to debase; lower; humiliate”), from Old High German *grollen, from Proto-Germanic *gruljaną (“to yell; shout at”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to grumble”). Compare English growl.

adj:gefleckt.tx: From Middle High German gevlecket, from Old High German giflekkōt. By surface analysis, ge- + Fleck + -t.

noun:Guacamole.tx: Borrowed from Spanish guacamole, from Classical Nahuatl āhuacamōlli.

noun:Gutachten.tx: From gut + achten first as a positive opinion, then generalized to any type of (expert) opinion.

noun:Gasthaus.tx: From Middle High German gasthūs, from Old High German gasthūs, from Proto-West Germanic *gastahūs, from Proto-Germanic *gastahūsą, equivalent to Gast (“guest”) + Haus (“house”). Compare Gästehaus.

noun:Gedärm.tx: From Middle High German gederme, from Old High German gidermi, from Proto-Germanic *gaþarmiją, collective of *þarmaz, whence German Darm.

verb:grapschen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?], from Middle Low German grabben (“to snap”), from Proto-Germanic *grab-, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (compare Sanskrit गृह्णाति (gṛhṇāti), गृभ्णाति (gṛbhṇāti, “he seizes”)).

noun:Graphit.tx: Ancient Greek γράφω (gráphō, “to write”) + -it (suffix for names of minerals)

verb:geizen.tx: From Middle High German gītesen, gīzen, from Old High German *gītisōn, from Proto-West Germanic *gīdisōn (“to be greedy for”). By surface analysis, Geiz (“stinginess”) + en.

noun:Gliederfüßer.tx: From Glied (“limb, joint”) + -er- + Fuß (“foot”) + -er (“-er”), literally “joint-footer”. Calque of translingual Arthropoda.

adj:gläsern.tx: From Glas (“glass”) + -ern or from Middle High German gleserīn, variant of glesīn, from Old High German glesīn, from Proto-West Germanic *glasīn.

noun:Gebilde.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?].

adj:gediegen.tx: From Middle High German gedigen (“mature, nourishing, capable”), from Old High German gidigan, githigan; originally the past participle of gedeihen (with Grammatischer Wechsel), making it a doublet of the modern, leveled past participle gediehen.

adj:geschmacklos.tx: Geschmack + -los. Compare Danish smagløs, Dutch smakeloos, English smackless.

noun:Getriebe.tx: Appears in the 1400s as a derivation from past participle getrieben of verb treiben.

adj:gewöhnungsbedürftig.tx: From Gewöhnung (“habituation”) + -s- + bedürftig (“in need (of)”). First attested in the 1970s.

noun:Glykolyse.tx: Ultimately from Ancient Greek γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”) + λύσις (lúsis, “a loosening”).

noun:Geber.tx: From geben + -er. Cognate with English giver.

noun:Gesichtspunkt.tx: Calque of French point de vue or earlier Latin punctum visus, from Gesicht + -s- + Punkt.

noun:Grüne.tx: Inherited from Middle High German grüene, from Old High German gruonī; equivalent to grün + -e (“ness”).

verb:gewöhnen.tx: From Middle High German gewenen, byform of gewennen, from Old High German giwennen, from Proto-West Germanic *gawannjan, prefixed form of *wannjan. Cognate with Dutch (ge)wennen, English wean. The ⟨ö⟩ is due to sporadic rounding of Middle High German /e/ in the vicinity of /ʃ/, /l/, and/or labials (cf. zwölf etc.). In this particular case, the development may have been reinforced by related words …

noun:Gestell.tx: From Middle High German gestelle, from Old High German gistelli.

noun:Gelächter.tx: From Middle High German gelehter, a collective form of Middle High German lahter, from Old High German lahtar, hlahtar (8th century), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”). Cognate with Old English hleahtor (whence English laughter) and Danish latter.

noun:Galmei.tx: Derived from Medieval Latin calamīna (or some Romance dialect), from Latin cadmia, ultimately from the Ancient Greek κᾰδμείᾱ, κᾰδμήᾱ, κᾰδμῐ́ᾱ (kădmeíā, kădmḗā, kădmĭ́ā, “calamine”).

noun:Gedränge.tx: From Middle High German, from Old High German gidrengi. Cognate with Old English ġeþrang.

noun:Grimm.tx: From Middle High German grim (“rage”), from the adjective grim, from Old High German grim, from Proto-Germanic *grimmaz (“fierce, grim”).

noun:Gewahrsam.tx: Nominalization of an adjective gewahrsam that faded in the 18th century, from gewahr + -sam.

noun:Genick.tx: From Middle High German genicke, collective of nac, nacke (whence modern Nacken). The -i- can be explained from underlying *genecke through influence of nicken (“to nod”). Alternatively, Middle High German genicke could be derived from the e-variant in Dutch nek, English neck (which is not attested in High German, however). Cognate with Hunsrik Gnick.

noun:Gewerbe.tx: From Middle High German gewerbe, from werben (German werben).

noun:Galgenvogel.tx: Galgen (“gallows”) + Vogel (“bird”). Compare English gallows bird and French gibier de potence.

verb:geruhen.tx: From Middle High German giruochen, from Old High German giruohhen, ruohhen, from Proto-Germanic *rōkijaną (“to take care”).

noun:Gutdünken.tx: Univerbation of earlier gut dünken, from Middle High German guotdunken.

adj:gewärtig.tx: gewarten + -ig, occasionally already Middle High German gewertec.

noun:Gefangener.tx: Substantivization of gefangen (“caught”). Compare Dutch gevangene.

adj:glitschig.tx: From glitschen (“to slip, slide”) + -ig. Probably ultimately related to glatt (“slippery, smooth, even”).

noun:Gotte.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Geliebter.tx: Substantivization of geliebt (“loved, beloved”), the past participle of lieben (“to love”).

noun:Gulden.tx: From Middle High German guldīn, gulden (“gold coin”, literally “golden”), from such forms as gulden pfenninc (“golden penny”), but especially from the gulden florīn (“golden florin”), a gold coin from Florence, which became popular in Germanic-speaking Europe since the late Middle Ages. Gulden was the predominant High German word for “golden”, though it was later supplanted by the variant forms …

noun:Gelbsucht.tx: From Middle High German gelsucht, gelsuht, from Old High German gelasuht, gelosuht, gelewasuht. By surface analysis, gelb + Sucht.

verb:gnaden.tx: From Middle High German genāden, from Old High German ginādōn. See Gnade (“mercy”).

adj:gefällig.tx: From Middle High German gevellic, gevellec, from Old High German gifellīg, synchronically analyzed as gefallen + -ig (DWDS).

adj:genügsam.tx: Partially from Middle High German genuhtsam, Old High German ginuhtsam from a noun ginuht f, but mostly secondarily after genugsam.

noun:Gatter.tx: From Middle High German gater, from Old High German gataro.

noun:Geselligkeit.tx: From Middle High German gesellekeit, gesellecheit. By surface analysis, gesellig + -keit.

adj:gesellig.tx: From Middle High German gesellec. By surface analysis, Geselle + -ig. Cognate with Dutch gezellig.

noun:Glaubhaftigkeit.tx: glaubhaft + -igkeit or alternatively from the dated German glaubhaftig, suffixed with -keit.

verb:gellen.tx: From Middle High German gëllen, from Old High German gëllan, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną (“to yell”). Cognate with English yell, Dutch gillen.

noun:Gemahl.tx: From Middle High German gemahel(e) (“bridegroom (bride)”), from Old High German gimahalo, from Old High German gimahalen (“to speak; (by extension) to be engaged under contract”), ultimately from Old High German mahal (“assembly; agreement, contract; covenant, marriage vows”).

verb:grübeln.tx: From Middle High German grübelen, from Old High German grubilōn, ultimately from the root of graben (“to dig”).

noun:Griesgram.tx: From Middle High German grisgramen (“to grind one’s teeth”), from Old High German grisgramōn (“to grind one’s teeth”). Later reanalyzed as a compound gries (“grey”) + Gram (“grief”), which influenced the semantic development, though the first element is instead related to Grieß (“semolina, grit”).

noun:Gespann.tx: From Middle High German gespan (“clasp; frame, welt”), from Old High German gespan (“clasp; chain, bracelet”), from Proto-Germanic *ga- + *spannaną. Equivalent to ge- (collective prefix) + spannen (“to span, yoke”). Cognate with Middle Dutch gespan (“clasp; pair; troup”), whence modern Dutch gespan, and Old English ġespan (“joining, fastening together; clasp; yoke”), whence probably modern …

noun:Großstädter.tx: From Großstadt + -er; analyzable as groß + Städter.

noun:Gehilfe.tx: From Middle High German gehëlfe, from Old High German gehëlfo.

adj:gläubig.tx: From Middle High German gelöubec, geloubec, from Old High German giloubīg. Equivalent to Glaube or glauben + -ig. Compare Dutch gelovig. While the verb was standardised with Upper German vocalism, the adjective continues the Central German form with umlaut against southern glaubig (cf. also abergläubisch).

noun:Gate.tx: Borrowed from English gate, ultimately Proto-Germanic *gatą. Doublet of regional Gatt (“hole, eye”), from Low German. Probably also related with inherited Gasse (“lane”).

verb:gammeln.tx: Borrowed from German Low German and Middle Low German gamelen, from Old Saxon *gamal (attested in the past participle gigamalōd), from Proto-Germanic *gamalaz (“weak, old”). Cognate to Old English gamolian. The verb pertains to an adjective meaning “old” attested in Middle Dutch gamel, Old English gamol, Old Norse gamall (whence forms in all modern Scandinavian languages).

noun:Gardinenpredigt.tx: Compound of Gardine (“curtain”) + Predigt (“sermon”). Probably a calque of Dutch gordijnpreek (an earlier form, now unused).

noun:Gelage.tx: Borrowed (and phonetically adapted) from Middle Low German gelach, gelōch. Pertaining to legen (“to lay”) and hence originally “food and drink laid on the table”. Now often associated more closely with liegen (“to lie”) and interpreted as “party where people lie down drunk”. Compare Dutch gelag.

noun:Gilde.tx: 17th century, from Middle Low German and Middle Dutch gilde. Related to Geld and gelten, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *geldan (“to pay”).

adj:glibberig.tx: From Middle Low German glibberich, from a Proto-Germanic base derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“to shine”). Compare Dutch glibberig, English glibbery.

verb:grabbeln.tx: From German Low German grabbelen, an expanded form of Middle Low German grabben. Related to Dutch grabbelen, English grab.

noun:Gracht.tx: Borrowed from Dutch gracht, which pertains to the cognate of German graben (“to dig”).

verb:grölen.tx: Via German Low German [Term?] from Middle Low German grālen, grölen.

noun:Gebärde.tx: From Middle High German gebærde, from Old High German gibārida, gibāridī (“demeanor, behavior, character”), from Proto-Germanic *gabērijaną, *gabarjaną (“to conduct oneself, behave”); see the related *gaberaną (“to bear, beget”) for more. Cognate with dialectal German Bärde, German Low German Gebarr, Dutch gebaarde, Middle English bærde, beard, beorde (“conduct, bearing”).

noun:Genus.tx: Borrowed from Latin genus. Doublet of Gender and Genre.

noun:Gestrüpp.tx: Derived from ge- + Middle High German struppe.

noun:Gehölz.tx: From Middle High German gehülze, from Old High German *gihulzī, from Proto-West Germanic *gahultī, from *hultī. Equivalent to ge- (collective noun forming prefix) + Holz (“wood”). Cognate with Middle Low German gehölte, Old English *hylte.

verb:greinen.tx: From Middle High German grīnen, from Old High German grīnan, from Proto-West Germanic *grīnan. Doublet of grienen.

adj:grässlich.tx: From Middle High German grēslich, from Middle Low German grēselîk (“horrific”), probably ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *grīsan (“to be frightened”), which is cognate with Old English grislic, whence English grisly. Cognate with Bavarian greißlich. In High German associated with unrelated graz (“angry”), from Old High German *graz (“strict”, attested as adverb grazzo), which is perhaps …

noun:Geschick.tx: From Middle High German geschicke (“occurrence, incident; disposition”), with semantic narrowing to "conditions and fate". See the related schicken (“to send”) for more.

noun:Gebrechen.tx: From Middle High German gebreche, gebrechen.

noun:Getöse.tx: Intensification of Middle High German dôz (“sound, noise, din”), ultimately derived from Middle High German diuzen, compare German tosen (“to roar, rage”) and Old English þys (“tempest, storm”).

noun:Gleichgültigkeit.tx: From gleichgültig + -keit, since the second half of the 17th century.

verb:grasen.tx: From Middle High German grasen, from Old High German grasōn, from Proto-West Germanic *grasōn. Equivalent to Gras (“grass”) + -en (verbal suffix). Cognate with English graze.

noun:Gehöft.tx: From Middle High German gehüfte, so attested 1309 in Königsdorf near Cologne; later also in East Central German gehoffte (and variants). Collective formation from Hof (“yard, farmyard, farm”). Regarding the Dutch colonisation in the east, it is possible that the German word goes back to Middle Dutch, in which ghehuchte, ghehochte, from Old Dutch *gihufti, is older and commoner. Plausibly the same …

noun:Gesuch.tx: From Middle High German gesuoh, from Old High German gisuoh.

noun:Grips.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?]. Derived with the suffix -s from Middle Low German grīpen or grabben. These interrelated verbs are cognate with English gripe and grab respectively. For the semantics compare German begreifen (“to understand”).

verb:gebieten.tx: From Middle High German gebieten, from Old High German gibiotan, equivalent to ge- + bieten. Cognate with Old English ġebēodan, Old Saxon gibiodan.

noun:Gebaren.tx: From Middle High German gebāren, from Old High German gibāren. Related to gebären (“to bear, give forth”).

verb:getrauen.tx: From Middle High German getrouwen, from Old High German gitrūwen. By surface analysis, ge- + trauen.

noun:Grind.tx: From Middle High German grint, from Old High German grint, from Proto-West Germanic *grind, from Proto-Germanic *grindą (“grounds, ground material”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrendʰ- (“to crush”). Cognate with West Frisian grint (“gravel”), Dutch grind (“gravel; shingle”), obsolete Dutch grinden (“to grind, rub, crush”). More at English grind. The sense for head developed metonymically as a clipping of Kopfgrind.

verb:gewahren.tx: From Middle High German gewarn, equivalent to gewahr + -en.

adj:gemächlich.tx: From Middle High German gemächlich, gemechlich, from Old High German gimahlīh, synchronically analyzed as gemach + -lich.

adj:grundlos.tx: From Middle High German gruntlōs. Equivalent to Grund (“ground”) + -los (“-less”).

noun:Gong.tx: Borrowed from English gong, from Malay gong.

noun:Gurgel.tx: From Middle High German gurgel, from Old High German gurgula, from Proto-West Germanic *gurgulā (“throat”).

noun:Gräuel.tx: From Middle High German griu(we)l, from the root of grauen (“to cause terror”).

phrase:guten Rutsch.tx: Literally, “good slide”, suggesting one slides into the new year. An alternative suggestion is that it derives from Hebrew רֹאשׁ (rosh, “beginning”), clipped from רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (rosh hashaná, “beginning of the new year”). (Compare Hals- und Beinbruch, said to be from a Yiddish phrase.)

noun:Gefieder.tx: From Middle High German gefidere, gevidere, gevider, extended forms of Middle High German fider, vider, *fidere, from Old High German fedari, *fidari, from Proto-Germanic *fiþriją.

noun:Grasmücke.tx: From Middle High German grasmucke, grasemucke, from Old High German grasamukka, grasamugga.

noun:Gnom.tx: Coined 1530 by Paracelsus as New Latin gnomus, of uncertain origin.

noun:Gelege.tx: From Middle High German gelēge, gelæge (“a lying, things lying about”), from Old High German *gilāgi, from Proto-Germanic *(ga)lēgiją, ablaut derivation from *ligjaną, whence liegen (“to lie”). Cognate with unprefixed Old Norse lægi. The form with ⟨e⟩ continues the older Central German spelling, reinforced by analogy with related legen (“to lay”); hence by surface analysis, ge- + legen + -e.

noun:Gymnastik.tx: 18th century, from Ancient Greek γυμναστική (gumnastikḗ), in part through Latin gymnastica.

adj:gottlos.tx: From Middle High German gotlōs. By surface analysis, Gott (“God”) + -los (“-less”)

adj:glaublich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German geloublich, from Old High German giloublīh. By surface analysis, glauben + -lich

noun:Geschütz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German geschütze, geschüz (“firearms, weapons”), collective noun of Middle High German schuʒ, schutz (“shot”). Not immediately related to schützen, geschützt.

noun:Gekröse.tx: From late Middle High German gekrœse (“(small) bowels”), itself a compound of ge- + krœs(e). Compare kraus, Middle Low German krȫse, Dutch croos (“bowels, entrails, guts”).

noun:Ger.tx: From Middle High German gēr, from Old High German gēr, from Proto-West Germanic *gaiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰoysós. By the time of Early New High German, it had largely been displaced by Speer in general usage. In the 19th century, there were ultimately unsuccessful attempts to revive the term outside of a historical context.

noun:Ginster.tx: From Middle High German ginster, from Old High German genester, byform of genesta, from Latin genista. The form in -r is probably from Old French genestre, an alteration of geneste; compare Italian ginestra. Further cognate with Dutch ginst.

noun:Gaube.tx: From late Middle High German gūpe. Further origin unknown. Since the word is apparently from Rhine Franconian dialects, identity with Kuppe (“top, knoll”), itself also a Central German form, is possible. The long vowel is problematic, however, though it might be due to conflation with a related word; compare Dutch kuif (“quiff, tuft of hair sticking out”), Old Norse kúfr (“knoll”). Alternatively, …

adj:glaubhaft.tx: From Middle High German geloubehaft, from Old High German giloubhaft. Equivalent to glauben + haft.

noun:Graupel.tx: 16th century. From Graupe (“hulled grain”) + -el (diminutive suffix). Graupe is from Slavic, where the senses “hulled grain” and “hail” are both present. Compare Polish krupa, Czech kroupa, Serbo-Croatian krupa.

verb:geringschätzen.tx: gering (“low, little”) + schätzen (“esteem”). Compare Dutch geringschatten.

noun:Gottesacker.tx: From Middle High German [Term?]. Equivalent to Gott + -es- + Acker. Cognate with East Central German gudsàger (Erzgebirgisch).

noun:Geschwulst.tx: From Middle High German geswulst, from Old High German giswulst, from the root of Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”).

verb:gruseln.tx: Replaced Middle High German griuseln; equivalent to grausen + -eln.

noun:Ganove.tx: 19th-century back-formation from the plural Ganoven, from Yiddish גנבֿים (ganóvim), itself plural of גנבֿ (gánev, “thief”), whence the dated German form above. Further from Hebrew גַּנָּב (gannāv).

noun:Gleiche.tx: From Middle High German gelīche, from Old High German gilīkī; equivalent to gleich + -e.

adj:gefiedert.tx: From Middle High German gevideret (past participle of videren), from Old High German gifiderit (past participle of fideren). By surface analysis, Gefieder + -t.

adj:geflissentlich.tx: From an earlier geflissenlich, from fleißen (“to strive”).

adj:geheuer.tx: From Middle High German gehiure (“pleasant, gentle”), from Old High German hiuri (“friendly, lovely”), from a suffixed form of or otherwise related to Proto-West Germanic *hīw (“marriage”).

adj:gelinde.tx: From Middle High German gelinde, equivalent to ge- + lind.

adj:gepfeffert.tx: From ge- + Pfeffer + -t or past participle of pfeffern.

adj:geschlechtsreif.tx: From Geschlecht + -s- + reif. Attested as early as the 19th century.

adj:gestiefelt.tx: From ge- + Stiefel + -t or past participle of stiefeln.

adj:geständig.tx: From Middle High German gestendec. See also Geständnis.

adj:getrost.tx: From Middle High German getrôst, from Old High German gitrōst. Etymologically comparable to a past participle of trösten, with ge-.

adv:getrost.tx: From Middle High German getrôst, from Old High German gitrōst. Etymologically comparable to a past participle of trösten, with ge-.

adj:glamourös.tx: From English glamorous. Equivalent to Glamour + -ös.

adj:glasklar.tx: From Glas (“glass”) + klar (“clear”). Compare English glass-clear, Swedish glasklar.

adj:gleichbedeutend.tx: From gleich + bedeutend or gleich + bedeuten + -end.

adj:glimpflich.tx: From Middle High German gelimpflich, from Old High German gilimpflīh, gilimphlīh, from Proto-West Germanic *galimpalīk. Cognate with Middle Low German gelimplīk, Old English ġelimplīċ. By surface analysis, derived from the obsolete noun Glimpf + -lich; compare Unglimpf.

adj:grasgrün.tx: From Middle High German grasgrüene, grasegrüene, from Old High German *grasagruoni, from Proto-West Germanic *grasagrōnī, from Proto-Germanic *grasagrōniz, equivalent to Gras + grün. Cognate with English grass-green.

adj:großkotzig.tx: According to the Kluge, the word is first attested in Berlin's 19th c. Hochsprache as an adjective synonymous with 'he who wins a pissing contest'. According to the Duden, the substantive Großkotz (“a bighead, a cocky person”) came first and out of Yiddish גרױסקצין (groyskotsn, “a filthy rich person or a pompous git”), derived in turn from קָצִין (katsín, “a leader or officer”), of uncertain …

noun:Geltung.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gëltunge, equivalent to gelten + -ung.

noun:Geschwader.tx: 16th century, from ge- (collective prefix) + Schwader. The latter is from Middle High German swader, from Italian squadra. The sense “group of birds” (16th century and thus predating aviation) is derived from the cavalry use.

noun:Geschmeide.tx: From Middle High German gesmide, from Old High German gismidi, collective formation of smīda (“metal”), related to smid (“blacksmith”).

intj:Gude.tx: Hessian pronunciation and shortening of guten Tag (“good day”).

noun:Grobian.tx: First attested in the 15th century in the form Grobianus, shortened by the 16th century. Humorous formation from grob (“coarse”) + Latin -iānus (“-ian”). Compare Schlendrian and further Dummerjan, Liederjan (also Dummrian, Liedrian).

noun:Gamba.tx: Borrowed from Spanish gamba and Catalan gamba.

noun:Grundel.tx: From Middle High German grundel, from Old High German grundila, variant of Old High German gruntila (“groundling”). Cognate with Luxembourgish Grondel, Dutch grondel, Old English grundling (English groundling).

phrase:Gott hab ihn selig.tx: Literally, “God have him in happiness”, or more loosely translated as “grant him heaven”.

phrase:Gott hab sie selig.tx: Literally, “God have her/them in happiness”, or more loosely translated as “grant her/them heaven”.

verb:gleißen.tx: From Middle High German glīȥen, from Old High German glīȥan, from Proto-Germanic *glītaną.

noun:Gischt.tx: From Middle High German jest, gest (“foam”), from Old High German *jest, *gest, from Proto-Germanic *jestuz (“fermentation; fermentative matter”). The form Gischt (instead of expected *Gest, *Jest) is probably onomatopoeic, though it could alternatively be of Alemannic German origin. Cognate with Dutch gist, English yeast.

noun:Gerte.tx: From Middle High German gerte, Old High German gartia (“rod, twig, staff”), from Proto-West Germanic *gaʀdi (“staff, rod, twig”). Cognates Cognate with English yard (“unit of measurement”), Saterland Frisian Jädde (“crop, yard”), Dutch garde (“whisk, stick, yard”). Also related to Old Norse gaddr, Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌶𐌳𐍃 (gazds), Latin hasta (“spear”).

noun:Gest.tx: Low German, from Middle Low German gest, from Old Saxon *gest, from, from Proto-West Germanic *jestu. Compare Dutch gist, English yeast, Swedish jäst, Icelandic jöstur.

adj:gesinnt.tx: From Middle High German gesinnet, gesint, formed as er- + sin + -et, equivalent to ge- + Sinn + -t.

adv:großenteils.tx: Univerbation of großen + Teils, adverbial genitive of großer Teil.

noun:Gröfaz.tx: Clipping of größter Feldherr aller Zeiten (“greatest commander-in-chief of all time”). First attested in 1943, apparently coined to mock Nazi Germany's love of long and obtuse abbreviations and Adolf Hitler's megalomania. The term was most likely coined in Berlin, where the word "Fatzke" was in common use to describe a thoroughly unpleasant, arrogant person, and the term was used to prevent …

noun:Gänze.tx: Middle High German genze, Old High German ganzi, corresponding to ganz + -e (“-ness”)

noun:Geheiß.tx: From Middle High German geheiȥe n, variant of geheiȥ m, from Old High German giheiȥ m, from Proto-Germanic *gahait-, deverbal from *haitaną, whence modern heißen (in the sense of “to command”).

noun:Gemütslage.tx: From Gemüt (“heart, soul, mind, disposition, temper”) + Lage (“situation”).

noun:Gender.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English gender. Doublet of Genre and Genus.

noun:Gspusi.tx: Borrowed from Italian sposo. Compare Alemannic German Gspuusi. Doublet of Gespons.

noun:Göffel.tx: Blend of Gabel (“fork”) + Löffel (“spoon”), probably after English spork, foon.

adj:genehm.tx: Inherited from Middle High German genæme, from Old High German gināmi, from Proto-West Germanic *ganāmī, a prefixed form of a verbal adjective from the root of nehmen (“to take”).

verb:gebühren.tx: From Middle High German gebürn, from Old High German giburien, giburren (first attested around 800), from Proto-West Germanic *gaburjan, from Proto-Germanic *gaburjaną. Compare Dutch gebeuren, from Old Dutch geburien (“to happen, occur”). See also Old Saxon giburian, Old English gebyrian, Old Norse byrja

noun:Geburtstagskind.tx: From Geburtstag (“birthday”) + -s- + Kind (“child”), literally “birthday kid”. Cognate with Silesian East Central German Geburtstagskind.

noun:Garaus.tx: Substantivized form of gar aus (“totally finished”, literally “completely out”). Compare English carouse.

noun:Glöckner.tx: From Middle High German glockenære, gloggenære, gloggener. Cognate with Middle Low German klöckenære. Glocke + -ner.

noun:Groove.tx: Borrowed from English groove. Doublet of Grube.

verb:grummeln.tx: From Low and Central German dialects, from Middle Low German grummelen and northern Middle High German *grummeln, iterative of grummen. A relation with Gram and grimmig is theoretically possible, but the words certainly have a strong onomatopoeic element. Cognate with Dutch grommelen, English grumble.

noun:Geläut.tx: From Middle High German geliute, equivalent to modern ge- + läuten (“to ring”).

noun:Gewaltmonopol.tx: From Gewalt (“force, violence”) + Monopol (“monopoly”). Coined by German sociologist and political economist Max Weber.

noun:Gründling.tx: Central and Low German alteration of the word in Grundel (now defined as “goby”), at first in Middle Low German grundelingk (early 15th c.).

noun:Gevatter.tx: From Middle High German gevatere, gevater, gefater, from Old High German gifatero (“godfather”), from Proto-West Germanic *gafaderjō, equivalent to ge- + Vater. Cognate with Old English ġefædera (“godfather”), Middle Low German gevādere, Dutch gevader, Yiddish קוואַטער (kvater). Compare also Medieval Latin compater. It is unclear whether the Germanic words were calqued from the Latin, or vice …

noun:Gelichter.tx: From Middle High German gelihter (“siblings, kin”), from Old High German lëhtar, gilëhtar (“womb, matrix”), a derivative of ligan, modern liegen (“to lie, to recline”). Since the seventeenth century often despective.

noun:Göttergatte.tx: Götter + Gatte, popularized via the operetta Der Göttergatte (The Divine Husband) by Franz Lehár (1904).

verb:gebrechen.tx: From Middle High German gebrechen, from Old High German gibrehhan.

noun:Gosche.tx: Unknown. Possibly from or related to Latin geusiae (“throat, maw”) or its descendants, compare Bavarian Goschn.

noun:Gartenstadt.tx: Calque of English garden city, Garten + Stadt.

verb:glucksen.tx: From Middle High German glucksen, iterative of glucken.

verb:glucken.tx: From Middle High German klucken, from Old High German klokkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *klukkwōn, from Proto-Germanic *klukkwōną, of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate with Dutch klokken, English cluck. The g- by dissimilation.

noun:Gebälk.tx: From Middle High German gebelke, collective of balke (“beam”). Equivalent to ge- + Balken.

noun:Gedöns.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Gedööns. Doublet of archaic Gedens. Popularized by a controversial remark made by Gerhard Schröder in the run-up to the 1998 German federal election (see quotations).

noun:Gemächt.tx: From Old High German gimaht, from Old High German gi- + maht.

noun:Gänger.tx: From Middle High German genger, from Old High German gangāri. Equivalent to Gang + -er.

noun:Glätte.tx: From Middle High German glete, earlier also gletī (12th c.). Equivalent to glatt + -e.

noun:Gänserich.tx: From Gans (“goose”) and/or Ganser (“gander”) + -rich (male suffix), by analogy with Enterich (which see). Compare Dutch ganzerik (“gander”), which is modelled after the German.

verb:gaukeln.tx: From Middle High German goukeln, from Old High German goukolon. See also Middle Low German gȫkelen, Middle Dutch gokelen, Old Dutch *gōkelen. Compare Dutch goochelen.

noun:Gezücht.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gezühte, equivalent to ge- + Zucht.

noun:Gästehaus.tx: From Gast (“guest”) + -e- + Haus (“house”). Compare Gasthaus. Cognate with English guesthouse.

noun:Gaudium.tx: Borrowed from Latin gaudium (“quiet, inner joy”), first only as part of Studentensprache, in which the semantic development happened. Attested since the 17th century in German texts, first with Latin inflection. Commonly known with the current meaning by the 18th century.

verb:glitzern.tx: From a frequentative form of Middle High German glitzen.

noun:Gefilde.tx: From Middle High German gevilde, from Old High German gifildi, from Proto-West Germanic *gafilþī, collective noun formed similarly to Berg → Gebirge.

noun:Gefälle.tx: From Middle High German gevelle, from Old High German gifelli, By surface analysis, ge- + fallen.

noun:Gallert.tx: East Central German form (17th c.) of Middle High German galreide, galrei (13th c.), from or related to Old Occitan gelareia, older Italian geleria (“aspic”). Ultimately from Latin gelu (“frost”).

noun:Gatt.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą. Cognate with Dutch gat, English gate. Doublet of Gate.

noun:Gaullismus.tx: Borrowed from French gaullisme; equivalent to de Gaulle + -ismus.

noun:Grundton.tx: Grund (“ground, base”) + Ton (“color, hue; tone, sound”)

noun:Gevögel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gevügele, from Old High German gifugili, equivalent to ge- + Vogel.

noun:Genussmittel.tx: Genuss (“pleasure, enjoyment”) + Mittel (“means, resource, substance”). Compare Dutch genotsmiddel (“recreational drug”)

verb:gedulden.tx: Middle High German [Term?], by surface analysis, ge- + dulden or rather by surface analysis, Geduld + -en.

pt: to form, to shape, to arrange
noun:Gestalter.tx: gestalten (“to form, to shape, to arrange”) + -er

noun:Glasnost.tx: Borrowed from Russian гла́сность (glásnostʹ, “openness”). The usual final stress is hyperforeign.

noun:Gulag.tx: Borrowed from Russian ГУЛА́Г (GULÁG): Гла́вное управле́ние исправи́тельно-трудовы́х лагере́й (Glávnoje upravlénije ispravítelʹno-trudovýx lageréj, “Chief Administration of Corrective-Labor Camps, Main Directorate for Places of Detention, Main Administration of Corrective Labor Camps, etc.”).

noun:Geograph.tx: From Latin geōgraphus. By surface analysis, geo- + -graph.

noun:Großmütigkeit.tx: From Middle High German grōʒmuotecheit, equivalent to großmütig (“magnanimous”) + -keit (“-ity”).

noun:Grundbuch.tx: From Grund (“ground, land”) + Buch (“book”), and grund- (“basic”) + Buch.

noun:Guide.tx: Borrowed from French guide and English guide, from Middle French guide, from Old French guide.

adj:gewahr.tx: From Middle High German gewar, from Old High German giwar, from Proto-West Germanic *gawar.

noun:Gepflogenheit.tx: gepflogen + -heit, the first part being the past participle of pflegen in its habitual meaning. The term emerged in 19th century Austrian bureaucratese.

noun:Gockel.tx: Attested 16th century, but probably older. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz, though similar forms exist independently in many languages. Ultimately onomatopoeic.

noun:Gettofaust.tx: Getto + Faust, likely due to being initially associated with lower-income urban communities in popular consciousness (compare English ghetto blaster). First attested in 2006, with more regular usage picking up in the 2010's.

adj:gewisslich.tx: Adjective: From Middle High German gewislich, gewislīch; equivalent to gewiss + -lich. Adverb: From Middle High German gewislīche (cp. gewislīchen, gewisselīchen), from Old High German giwislīhho; equivalent to gewiss + -lich.

adv:gewisslich.tx: Adjective: From Middle High German gewislich, gewislīch; equivalent to gewiss + -lich. Adverb: From Middle High German gewislīche (cp. gewislīchen, gewisselīchen), from Old High German giwislīhho; equivalent to gewiss + -lich.

noun:Gamander.tx: From Middle High German gamandrē, from Late Latin gamandrea, chamandrea, from Latin chamaedrys, from Ancient Greek χαμαίδρῡς (khamaídrūs, literally “ground-oak”).

noun:Gebell.tx: From Middle High German gebelle. By surface analysis, ge- + bellen.

noun:Gebräu.tx: From Middle High German gebriu, gebriuwe.

noun:Gelüst.tx: Middle High German gelüste, Old High German gilusti, related to gelüsten.

verb:gelüsten.tx: From Middle High German gelüsten, gelusten, glusten, from Old High German gilusten, from Proto-West Germanic *galustijan, equivalent to ge- + lüsten. Cognate with Middle Low German gelüsten, Middle Dutch gelusten, Saterland Frisian gelustje, Old English ġelystan (“to please, desire, like”).

adj:genugsam.tx: From Middle High German genuocsam, from Old High German ginuogsam, equivalent to genug + -sam.

noun:Gestik.tx: Borrowed from Latin gesticulus, diminutive of gestus.

noun:Gemme.tx: Borrowed from Italian gemma (“bud, gem”). Replaced Middle High German gimme, from Old High German gimma.

noun:Gewölle.tx: Inherited from Middle High German gewel, gewelle, from Middle High German wullen, wüllen, willen (“to vomit”), from Old High German willōn, wullōn. Not related to German Wolle.

noun:Game.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English game, ellipsis of video game.

noun:Gaudi.tx: Since the 19th century, from Gaudium, from Latin gaudium.

noun:Gondoliere.tx: Unadapted borrowing from Italian gondoliere. Doublet of Gondolier.

noun:Geflüchteter.tx: From geflüchtet, past participle of flüchten.

noun:Gunsten.tx: From the archaic plural of Gunst.

adj:gastlich.tx: From Middle High German gastlich, from Old High German gastlīh. Equivalent to Gast + -lich. Compare English guestly.

noun:Gack.tx: Spelling variant of Kack reflecting the pronunciation. An onomatopoeic creation relating to the sound a baby makes when pressing while defecating (“a-a-”); compare Aa machen as well as Latin cacō, Ancient Greek κακκάω (kakkáō).

noun:Glosse.tx: From Middle High German glōse, from Late Latin glōssa. The modern spelling with -ss- is from renewed influence by the Latin spelling in the 17th century, despite maintaining the pronunciation with /oː/ in technical usage.

noun:Galgenstrick.tx: Middle High German galgenstric, by surface analysis, Galgen (“gallows”) + Strick (“rope”).

noun:Gehänge.tx: From Middle High German gehenge. Equivalent to ge- (collective prefix) + hängen (“to hang”).

noun:Generalgouvernement.tx: From general- (“general”) + Gouvernement (“governorate, provisional administrative unit”).

phrase:gehüpft wie gesprungen.tx: Literally, “[just as well] hopped as jumped”.

noun:Gassenhauer.tx: Since the 16th century, originally in the literal meaning "someone who walks on alleys" as well as the figurative meaning "song sung on alleys" but without derogatory connotations. By surface analysis, Gasse (“alley”) + -n- + hauen (“to tread”, literally “to beat”) + -er.

noun:Gebein.tx: From Middle High German gebeine, from Old High German gibeini. Equivalent to ge- + Bein.

adj:grauslich.tx: From Middle High German grūslich, grūsenlich. By surface analysis, grausen + -lich.

noun:Geometer.tx: From Late Latin geōmetrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs).

intj:geilomat.tx: Fanciful extension of geil, probably through the form geilo; perhaps inspired by Automat.

phrase:gut gebrüllt, Löwe.tx: Literally, “well roared, lion”, from August Wilhelm Schlegel's translation of A Midsummer Night's Dream.

intj:Glückauf.tx: Short for Ich wünsche Dir Glück, tu einen neuen Gang auf (“I wish you luck, open a new lode”). It describes the hope of the miners: es mögen sich Erzgänge auftun (“may lodes [of ore] be opened”).

noun:Genital.tx: Borrowed from Latin genitālis (“of or belonging to generation”), from genitus, past participle of gignō (“to beget, generate”); see genus.

noun:Genitale.tx: Borrowed from Latin genitālis (“of or belonging to generation”), from genitus, past participle of gignō (“to beget, generate”); see genus.

noun:Geiselhaft.tx: From Geisel (“hostage”) + Haft (“captivity”). The latter word retains its broader sense here, having otherwise become widely restricted to “legal arrest, imprisonment”.

noun:Gegenbesuch.tx: Calque of French contre-visite, gegen- + Besuch.

noun:Gewissensfreiheit.tx: From Gewissen + -s- + Freiheit. A calque of Latin libertas conscientiae (“freedom of conscience”).

noun:Gusto.tx: Borrowed from Italian gusto, from Latin gustus (“tasting”), from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.

phrase:guten Durst.tx: Ellipsis of ich wünsche dir einen guten Durst (“I wish you a good thirst”).

noun:Gemeinsinn.tx: 17th century, from gemein + Sinn, a calque of Latin sensus communis. The Latin means “common sense”, but does allow the reinterpretation insofar as communis means both “common” and “communal”. The meaning appeared in German since the 18th century and had displaced the original one by the mid-19th.

noun:Genpool.tx: Gen + Pool; calque of English gene pool.

noun:Glibber.tx: Back-formation from glibberig (“slimy”). Cognate with English glib, archaic glibbery.

noun:Grünland.tx: From grün + Land. In the obsolete geographic sense ultimately a calque of Old Norse Grœnland.

noun:Gehhilfe.tx: From gehen (“to go, to walk”) + Hilfe (“help”).

noun:Gaststar.tx: Gast + Star. Possibly a calque of English guest star.

noun:Geratewohl.tx: Univerbation of gerate wohl, literally “come out well” (imperative).

noun:Gnadenakt.tx: From Gnade + Akt. Equivalent to “act of mercy” or “act of grace”.

noun:Glefe.tx: From Middle High German glævîn, glevie, gleve (since approx. 1200)

noun:Grillparty.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from grill + party. Compare Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish grillparty.

noun:Geschnetzeltes.tx: Nominalization of geschnetzelt, past participle of schnetzeln (“to slice”).

adj:gehirnamputiert.tx: Gehirn (“brain”) + amputiert (“amputated”), playing off the same idea as hirnlos or English brainless. Küpper dates it to the 1960s, attested in writing by the 1970s.

noun:Gesundheitsversicherung.tx: Gesundheit + -s- + Versicherung, perhaps a calque of English health insurance.

noun:Gehtnichtmehr.tx: Nominalization of the phrase (es) geht nicht mehr (“it won't work any more; it can't be done anymore”).
